title: Homological Thresholds In Randomly Monitored Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
authors: Yoshito Watanabe, Daiki Sasamoto, Bo Han, Simon Trebst
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random projective measurements are an effective tool to model the interlinked phenomenology of monitoring, inferring, and decoding highly entangled states such as quantum error-correcting codes. At the same time, the study of such monitored dynamics has opened a new arena for critical phenomena, renewing longstanding questions in disordered statistical mechanics, including percolation, random-bond models, and Nishimori physics. Here we investigate the robustness of stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes under a single round of independently sampled single-qubit Pauli measurements and demonstrate that their threshold behavior falls into two broad categories - geometric and homological percolation transitions, with the toric code and color code being the principal examples for each class. We establish the distinct character of these two threshold theories by analyzing the logical-support criteria of these codes and by providing numerical estimates of their respective critical exponents obtained from optimized stabilizer simulations of large-scale systems with over one million qubits. Our framework extends to non-CSS, subsystem, higher-dimensional, and Floquet stabilizer codes and allows us to determine their respective threshold phase diagrams. We exemplify how the latter provide quantitative and qualitative guidance for the computationally more demanding problems of tunable learning and maximum-likelihood decoding. As a practical application of our framework, we discuss the robustness of the gross code.
tldr: The paper classifies threshold behavior of stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes under random single-qubit Pauli measurements into geometric and homological percolation transitions, exemplified by the toric and color codes.
motivation: Random projective measurements provide a model for monitoring, decoding, and critical phenomena in highly entangled quantum codes, but the robustness and threshold classification of stabilizer codes under such measurements remain incompletely understood.
method: The authors analyze logical-support criteria for stabilizer codes and perform optimized stabilizer simulations of systems with over one million qubits to estimate critical exponents and threshold phase diagrams.
result: They identify two distinct threshold classes—geometric and homological percolation transitions—with the toric and color codes as principal examples, and extend the framework to non-CSS, subsystem, higher-dimensional, and Floquet stabilizer codes.
conclusion: The framework offers quantitative guidance for tunable learning and maximum-likelihood decoding, and is applied to discuss the robustness of the gross code.

title: Resource Theory Of Aquaternionicity: Every Pure State Is A Replicable Resource For Exact Simulation Of Arbitrary Quantum Operations
authors: Yasuaki Nakayama Hayato Arai
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An alchemical resource theory admits a nonfree state that can be exactly replicated by free operations and whose finitely many copies enable exact simulation of arbitrary quantum instruments. The only known nontrivial examples, imaginarity and parity asymmetry, exhaust the qubit case (arXiv:2609.12988) and exhibit an all-or-nothing property: any nonmaximal resource exactly simulates only free unitaries. We introduce aquaternionicity for even-dimensional qudits [MATH], based on a quaternionic structure represented by an antiunitary [MATH] with [MATH]. It is extremal in two senses: every pure state is alchemical, and alchemicality is maximally abundant under mixing. Within this framework, for any nontrivial [MATH]-dimensional resource theory and pure alchemical state [MATH], the admissible pure-mixing set satisfies [MATH] which aquaternionicity saturates for every pure state. Conversely, these two extremal properties characterize the quaternionic structure. Because every pure state is alchemical, the initial resource can be chosen to match the known noise structure. Moreover, when the noisy resource states remain within a common isotropic subspace, the same free processor works exactly for all of them while returning the resource unchanged. This enables recalibration-free exact simulation, including universal quantum computation, and is realized for standard dephasing and dissipative noise, where aquaternionicity substantially outperforms imaginarity and parity asymmetry.
tldr: Introduces aquaternionicity, a quaternionic resource theory for even-dimensional qudits in which every pure state is alchemical and enables exact simulation of arbitrary quantum instruments.
motivation: Existing alchemical resource theories such as imaginarity and parity asymmetry only exhaust the qubit case and exhibit an all-or-nothing behavior, motivating a more abundant resource that supports exact simulation beyond qubits.
method: Defines aquaternionicity via an antiunitary quaternionic structure, analyzes extremal properties of the admissible pure-mixing set, and studies exact simulation of quantum instruments under standard dephasing and dissipative noise.
result: Aquaternionicity is shown to saturate the pure-mixing bound for every pure state and to enable recalibration-free exact simulation, including universal quantum computation, substantially outperforming imaginarity and parity asymmetry.
conclusion: The quaternionic structure is characterized by two extremal properties, yielding a powerful resource theory for noise-robust exact simulation of arbitrary quantum operations.

title: Random Quantum Ldpc Codes Approaching The Gilbert-Varshamov Bound
authors: Tushant Mittal, Shashank Srivastava, Madhur Tulsiani, Mary Wootters
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that for any [MATH] and any prime [MATH], there exists an infinite family of [MATH]-ary quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes, rate [MATH], checks of weight [MATH], and normalized distance at least [MATH]. Here, [MATH] denotes the quantum Gilbert-Varshamov (GV) bound for [MATH]-ary stabilizer codes. In fact, we construct an ensemble of such QLDPC codes, such that a random code from this ensemble is close to the GV bound with high probability. Moreover, this ensemble matches the performance of random stabilizer codes on several quantum channels. Specifically, it approaches the quantum capacity of the erasure channel and the hashing bound for memoryless Pauli channels, including the depolarizing channel. A significant challenge in working with QLDPC codes is that they are necessarily , i.e., contain many low-weight stabilizers. A key contribution of our work is a construction of QLDPC codes with quantitative control on their degeneracy. These codes are obtained by combining known constructions of asymptotically good QLDPC codes with the expander-based distance amplification procedure of Alon, Edmonds, and Luby [FOCS'95]. Our random ensemble is constructed by starting with these low-degeneracy QLDPC codes near the quantum Singleton bound and concatenating each coordinate with a random inner code. This can be viewed as a quantum analogue of Thommesen's construction, and as an LDPC version of a result of Ouyang, with an appropriately designed outer code.
tldr: The paper constructs random quantum LDPC codes that approach the quantum Gilbert-Varshamov bound and match random stabilizer code performance on several quantum channels.
motivation: Quantum LDPC codes are promising for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but achieving the quantum Gilbert-Varshamov bound with sparse checks has been a longstanding challenge, partly due to uncontrolled degeneracy.
method: The authors combine asymptotically good QLDPC codes with expander-based distance amplification and then concatenate each coordinate with a random inner code, yielding a random ensemble with quantitative control over degeneracy.
result: They obtain q-ary QLDPC codes with rate and normalized distance asymptotically approaching the quantum GV bound, and show the ensemble approaches the quantum capacity of the erasure channel and the hashing bound for Pauli channels.
conclusion: This provides a quantum analogue of Thommesen's construction and demonstrates that random QLDPC codes can be near-optimal for quantum error correction and channel coding.

deep_read.detailed_summary:
This paper establishes the existence of p-ary quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes that achieve the quantum Gilbert-Varshamov (GV) bound for stabilizer codes. Specifically, for any rate R, any ε>0, and any prime p≥2, the authors construct an infinite family of QLDPC codes with rate R, checks of constant weight O_ε(1), and normalized distance at least δ_GV(p,R) - ε. The construction yields an ensemble of such codes where a random member is close to the GV bound with high probability. Moreover, this ensemble matches the performance of random stabilizer codes on several quantum channels: it approaches the quantum capacity of the erasure channel and the hashing bound for memoryless Pauli channels, including the depolarizing channel.

A central challenge in QLDPC codes is their inherent degeneracy—the presence of many low-weight stabilizers—which complicates distance analysis and performance guarantees. The authors address this by first constructing QLDPC codes with quantitative control on degeneracy. They combine known asymptotically good QLDPC codes with the expander-based distance amplification procedure of Alon, Edmonds, and Luby (FOCS'95). This yields low-degeneracy QLDPC codes near the quantum Singleton bound. The random ensemble is then built by concatenating each coordinate of these outer codes with a random inner code, analogous to Thommesen's classical construction and an LDPC version of Ouyang's result.

The paper's main technical achievement is showing that this concatenated ensemble achieves the GV bound while maintaining constant check weight and controlled degeneracy. The analysis leverages properties of expander graphs for distance amplification and random coding arguments for the inner codes. The results imply that QLDPC codes can be as good as random stabilizer codes for several important quantum channels, bridging a gap between practical LDPC constructions and information-theoretic limits.
key_contributions: Existence of p-ary QLDPC codes achieving the quantum Gilbert-Varshamov bound with constant check weight and rate R, for any prime p and any ε>0.
Construction of a random ensemble of QLDPC codes that is close to the GV bound with high probability and matches random stabilizer code performance on erasure and Pauli channels.
A method to quantitatively control degeneracy in QLDPC codes by combining asymptotically good QLDPC codes with expander-based distance amplification.
A quantum analogue of Thommesen's construction and an LDPC version of Ouyang's result, using concatenation with random inner codes.
Demonstration that the ensemble approaches the quantum capacity of the erasure channel and the hashing bound for depolarizing and other memoryless Pauli channels.

For the first, the authors start with known asymptotically good QLDPC codes (likely from recent breakthroughs) and apply the Alon-Edmonds-Luby distance amplification procedure using expander graphs. This procedure amplifies the distance while preserving the LDPC property and controlling the number of low-weight stabilizers. The resulting outer codes are near the quantum Singleton bound and have quantitative degeneracy control. For the second, each coordinate of the outer code is replaced by a random inner code (a random stabilizer code of small length). This concatenation yields a random QLDPC code ensemble. The analysis then shows that with high probability, a random code from this ensemble has distance approaching the GV bound. The proof likely uses probabilistic methods to bound the weight enumerator and employs the degeneracy control to handle the quantum case. The connection to Thommesen's classical construction suggests a similar random coding argument adapted to the quantum setting, with careful handling of entanglement and degeneracy.

It advances the understanding of QLDPC codes, which are promising for fault-tolerant quantum computing due to their constant check weight and high rate. title: Analytical Controls For Dispersive Multi-qubit Interactions In Mediator-coupled Quantum Registers
authors: Bora Baran, Tommaso Calarco, James O'sullivan, Matthias M. M\"uller, Felix Motzoi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast control of long-lived quantum registers often relies on an auxiliary degree of freedom, a mediator, but real mediator excitation can introduce decoherence, leakage, or loss when the mediator is not the coherence-optimized component. We introduce dispersive interaction via analytical linear inversion (DIAL), an analytical control construction for excitation-suppressed interaction engineering in mediator-coupled quantum registers. In the dispersive regime, we show that off-resonant driving of an effective two-level mediator transition yields a diagonal Hamiltonian whose Pauli-\(Z\) interaction rates depend linearly on the drive intensities through a transfer matrix determined by the register-resolved transition spectrum. This establishes a direct linear map from experimentally accessible controls to induced multi-qubit interactions, enabling control design without iterative propagation of the full driven dynamics. We turn this structure into the target-aware DIAL algorithm, which selects favorable off-resonant tones and determines their drive intensities for a prescribed target interaction. We benchmark the resulting controls across 100 register realizations for each register size \(n=2,3,4,5\), targeting the highest-order interaction \(Z_1\cdots Z_n\) with an interaction phase of magnitude \(\pi/4\), which generates an \(n\)-qubit GHZ state up to local equivalence. Propagation under the full driven mediator-register dynamics yields typical gate fidelities above \(0.997\), while the maximum transient mediator excitation remains near \(1\%\) on average, far below what is typically possible with resonant Rabi drives. The manuscript is accompanied by an open-source Python package implementing the target-aware DIAL algorithm and the associated numerical validation workflow.
tldr: Introduces DIAL, an analytical control method for engineering target multi-qubit interactions in mediator-coupled quantum registers while suppressing mediator excitation.
motivation: Fast control of long-lived quantum registers often relies on a mediator, but real mediator excitation can cause decoherence, leakage, or loss when the mediator is not coherence-optimized.
method: In the dispersive regime, off-resonant driving of an effective two-level mediator transition yields a diagonal Hamiltonian whose Pauli-Z interaction rates depend linearly on drive intensities through a transfer matrix; the target-aware DIAL algorithm selects favorable tones and intensities for a prescribed target interaction.
result: Benchmarks across 100 register realizations for n=2,3,4,5 targeting the highest-order Z1...Zn interaction with phase π/4, which generates an n-qubit GHZ state up to local equivalence, show typical gate fidelities above 0.997 and maximum transient mediator excitation near 1% on average.
conclusion: DIAL provides an analytical control construction for mediator-coupled quantum registers, enabling high-fidelity multi-qubit interactions with low mediator excitation, and is accompanied by an open-source Python implementation.

title: Singer-Difference-Set Qudit Stabilizer Codes From Non-Degenerate Quadrics In PG(d,q)PG(d,q): Construction, Structural Theorems, And Monte-Carlo Performance

abstract: ArXiv:2610.02392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose Q(q,d), a family of q-ary non-CSS qudit stabilizer codes with prime power q and dimension d >= 2, constructed from Singer difference sets and non-degenerate quadrics in PG(d,q). The parity check H = (A | M_Q A) couples the Singer-circulant incidence matrix A with the quadric circulant M_Q, and a Cancellation Lemma uses the identity (k - lambda) = q^{d-1} = 0 mod p to make H symplectic-isotropic over F_q. Five structural theorems carry the novelty: a cross-correlation modular-constancy identity nu = 1 mod q at q odd, d >= 3, with a two-value pattern that proves a 2-torsion distance ceiling; a CRT zero-count identity; an explicit Clifford bridge identifying Q(q,2) as a graph-state encoding of the trivial Singer CSS code, with the 2021 low-density-spreading (LDS) sign-flip pattern realised by a symmetric circulant; a paired column-rigidity equality d_min = R_P + 1; and a lower bound d_min(Q(7,2)) >= 8 from an exhaustive Singer-Frobenius search. A Hamada-Smith specialisation yields the closed-form logical dimension k(p,d) = theta_d(p) - C(p+d-1, d) - 1, and the flagship Q(p,2) = [[p^2 + p + 1, p(p+1)/2, d_min]]_p attains asymptotic rate one-half. We conjecture d_min(Q(p,2)) = p + 1 for odd primes, proven at p = 5 and lower-bounded to >= 8 at p = 7. Instances include Q(3,2) = [[13,6,3]]_3, Q(5,2) = [[31,15,6]]_5, Q(7,2) = [[57,28, d>=8]]_7, and Q(3,4) = [[121,105,3]]_3. Monte-Carlo over 1.5 x 10^6 trials shows Q(5,2) achieves a 70-fold per-logical-qudit improvement over Steane [[7,1,3]]_2 at depolarising rate 10^-3 with zero silent logical errors. A textbook bounded-distance decoder is used; Berlekamp-Massey-style cyclic decoding is left as the natural sequel.
tldr: The paper constructs a family of q-ary non-CSS qudit stabilizer codes from Singer difference sets and non-degenerate quadrics in projective geometry, providing structural theorems and Monte-Carlo performance benchmarks.
motivation: Quantum error correction for qudits requires stabilizer codes with good parameters, efficient construction, and practical decoding performance beyond the qubit case.
method: The authors define parity checks H = (A | M_Q A) using Singer-circulant incidence matrices and quadric circulants, prove symplectic isotropy via a Cancellation Lemma, derive five structural theorems, and evaluate performance with a bounded-distance decoder and Monte-Carlo simulations.

conclusion: Singer-difference-set quadric codes offer a promising route to high-rate qudit stabilizer codes, with a conjectured distance d_min(Q(p,2)) = p + 1 and future work on Berlekamp-Massey-style cyclic decoding.

title: High-Rate Quantum Codes With Proven Distance And Low-Weight Measurements
authors: Kishor Bharti, Tobias Haug, Runzhou Tao, Kevin Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a family of quantum subsystem codes defined on rectangular coordinate grids of any dimension, with even side lengths of at least four. The directly measured operators act along coordinate lines. For every member of the family, we derive the number of protected logical qubits and prove its dressed distance without a numerical search. To illustrate the resulting design choices, we impose a budget of at most 10,000 data qubits and determine the complete tradeoff between encoding rate and measurement weight within this family at distances 16, 32, and 64. At distance 16, one code protects 4,096 logical qubits among 10,000 data qubits using weight-ten measurements. At distances 32 and 64, codes with 7,776 and 9,216 data qubits protect 1,024 and 256 logical qubits, respectively, using weight-six measurements. We include and explain Lean code snippets throughout the paper to guide readers through the formal verification of our subsystem-code construction and its dressed and bare distances.
tldr: The paper introduces a family of quantum subsystem codes on rectangular grids with proven distance and low-weight measurements, achieving high encoding rates under a qubit budget.
motivation: To design quantum error correction codes with high rate, low measurement weight, and provable distance, which is crucial for scalable quantum computing.
method: They define subsystem codes on coordinate grids, derive logical qubit counts, prove dressed and bare distances, and use Lean for formal verification.
result: At distance 16, a code with 10,000 data qubits protects 4,096 logical qubits using weight-10 measurements; at distances 32 and 64, codes achieve 1,024 and 256 logical qubits with weight-6 measurements.
conclusion: The family provides a tradeoff between encoding rate and measurement weight, enabling efficient quantum error correction with formal verification.

title: Gaussian Fisher Information Is Superadditive
authors: Jiaxin Liu, Zuoxian Wang, Danyue Ma
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Fisher information adds over independent probes, so a single parameter is best measured probe by probe. We show that Gaussian measurements, the linear optics and homodyne detection of optical and microwave experiments, break this rule: two independent modes are better measured together. The uncertainty principle leaves a linear detector half of phase space, and for two modes the choice of half is a resource. Bell homodyne, a balanced beam splitter followed by two homodyne detectors, beats the best separate readout when the modes differ in quadrature width and in how the width responds to the parameter. Heterodyne detection splits a mode on a beam splitter to read both quadratures and pays one unit of vacuum noise for the empty port. Bell homodyne fills that port with the second mode, so the noise turns into signal. We prove that the gain stays below [MATH] for every parameter carried by widths. For thermal modes at one temperature, the canonical case, a gain was conjectured impossible. We prove that any frequency difference opens a temperature window and that the gain peaks at [MATH] at frequency ratio [MATH], where Bell homodyne is the optimal Gaussian measurement. Standard hardware reaches the gain: two coupled resonators with two homodyne detectors, or a phase-preserving amplifier whose idler band is fed by the same thermal source.
tldr: The paper proves that Gaussian measurements can yield superadditive quantum Fisher information, with Bell homodyne beating separate readout for two independent bosonic modes.
motivation: Quantum Fisher information normally adds over independent probes, suggesting separate measurements are optimal; the authors ask whether Gaussian measurements can break this additivity and provide a resource for joint estimation.
method: They analyze Gaussian measurements on two modes, including Bell homodyne (a beam splitter plus two homodyne detectors), derive bounds on the gain, and prove optimality for thermal modes with a frequency difference.
result: Bell homodyne outperforms the best separate readout when modes differ in quadrature width and parameter response; for thermal modes any frequency difference opens a temperature window for gain, peaking at a specific frequency ratio where Bell homodyne is the optimal Gaussian measurement.
conclusion: Gaussian Fisher information is superadditive, and the effect is experimentally accessible with coupled resonators and homodyne detectors or a phase-preserving amplifier with an idler band.

The authors show that for Gaussian measurements—specifically linear optics and homodyne detection—two independent modes can be better measured together than separately. The key insight is that the uncertainty principle restricts a linear detector to half of phase space, and for two modes the choice of which half to measure becomes a resource. They introduce 'Bell homodyne', a scheme where a balanced beam splitter mixes the two modes before two homodyne detectors. This setup outperforms the best separate readout when the modes differ in quadrature width and in how that width responds to the parameter. Heterodyne detection, which splits a mode to read both quadratures, pays one unit of vacuum noise; Bell homodyne fills that empty port with the second mode, converting noise into signal. The authors prove that the gain is bounded by (√2−1)² ≈ 17.157% for any parameter encoded in quadrature widths. For thermal modes at a single temperature—a canonical case where gain was conjectured impossible—they show that any frequency difference opens a temperature window, with a peak gain of 12.699% at a frequency ratio of 3.318, where Bell homodyne is the optimal Gaussian measurement. They also propose feasible implementations using coupled resonators or a phase-preserving amplifier with an idler band fed by the same thermal source.

They model the two independent modes as Gaussian states characterized by their quadrature variances and the dependence of these variances on the parameter of interest. The measurement schemes considered are restricted to Gaussian measurements, specifically homodyne detection, heterodyne detection, and the proposed Bell homodyne (a beam splitter followed by two homodyne detectors). The performance metric is the quantum Fisher information (QFI) or the classical Fisher information for the specific measurement, and the gain is defined as the ratio of the joint estimation precision to the best separate estimation precision. The authors derive analytical bounds on the gain by optimizing over the beam splitter transmissivity and the local oscillator phases. For the thermal case, they consider two modes with different frequencies but the same temperature, and they optimize the gain over the frequency ratio and the temperature. They also identify the optimal Gaussian measurement by comparing the QFI of Bell homodyne to the full Gaussian QFI. The proofs are supplemented by numerical evaluations to find the maximum gain and the corresponding parameters.

title: Thermalization In A Repeated-interaction Model With Memory Effects
authors: Kanji Nishii, Ryo Nagai, Yoshihiko Abe
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how memory affects the thermalization of a qubit in a repeated-interaction model. In our model, a memory qubit interacts repeatedly with the system, while both qubits undergo collisions with fresh thermal ancillas. We derive exact closed evolution equations for their populations and mutual coherence, and demonstrate memory effects using a causal-break operation. Although the system converges to the target thermal state, the thermalization behavior shows non-monotonic approach. We also find a Mpemba-like reversal, in which the number of collisions required for thermalization depends non-monotonically on the temperature of the target state. Within the initial-state family considered, both phenomena require initial coherence between the system and memory or an imbalance in their excited-state populations.
tldr: The paper studies how memory affects thermalization of a qubit in a repeated-interaction model, finding non-monotonic relaxation and a Mpemba-like reversal in the number of collisions needed to thermalize.
motivation: Memory effects in open quantum systems can qualitatively alter thermalization and relaxation, but their role in collision models and anomalous phenomena like the Mpemba effect is not fully understood.
method: The authors derive exact closed evolution equations for the populations and mutual coherence of a system qubit and a memory qubit that repeatedly collide with fresh thermal ancillas, and they use a causal-break operation to isolate memory effects.
result: Although the system converges to the target thermal state, the approach is non-monotonic, and the number of collisions required for thermalization depends non-monotonically on the target temperature, producing a Mpemba-like reversal that requires initial system-memory coherence or an excited-state population imbalance.
conclusion: Memory and initial correlations can significantly modify thermalization dynamics in repeated-interaction models, revealing anomalous relaxation effects relevant to quantum thermodynamics and open quantum systems.

title: Noncommutative Marcus-Ree Inequality And Erd\H{o}s Channels
authors: Chaman Kumar Sahu Repana Devendra
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unital quantum channels are the noncommutative analogues of doubly stochastic matrices. In 1959, Marcus and Ree showed that the squared Frobenius norm of a doubly stochastic matrix is at most its maximal diagonal sum. We prove a quantum version of this inequality for mixed unitary channels on [MATH] and give an example showing that it fails for general unital channels. As in the classical case, we call the channels attaining equality as Erds channels. We show that the trace-preserving conditional expectation onto any unital [MATH]-subalgebra of [MATH] is an Erds channel. It is also locally isolated among channels of the same Choi rank. Next, we introduce quantum RCDS channels. These are the noncommutative analogue of doubly stochastic matrices whose supported permutations all have the same diagonal sum. We prove a structure theorem for them and use it to characterize the quantum RCDS Erds channels. We give an explicit form, up to unitary equivalence, for the Erds channels of Choi rank [MATH], and further show that there are uncountably many unitary equivalence classes of Erds channels unlike the classical case. We also characterize the Erds channels among mixed Weyl-unitary channels of any Choi rank. For qubits, we prove that there are exactly four unitary equivalence classes of Erds channels and they are represented by the identity channel and uniform averages of Pauli channels. Finally, restricting to the diagonal channels, our results recover the Marcus--Ree inequality, the structure of RCDS doubly stochastic matrices, and the characterization of Erds.

title: Gap-Protected Heisenberg-Limited Squeezing With Locally Interacting Multi-Level Spins
authors: Sakshi Bahamnia, Sagar Chaudhary, Arman Duha, Thomas Bilitewski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02314v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate a general mechanism to generate scalable, metrologically useful entanglement in the form of generalized spin squeezing in multi-level (qudit) spin systems with power-law interactions. We demonstrate this for spin-changing dynamics, extending the physics of spin-nematic squeezing known from spinor BECs to spatially extended lattice geometries. In the absence of all-to-all connectivity, the dynamics generally suffers from leakage into non-collective finite-momentum modes, destroying Heisenberg scaling. We show that introducing local [MATH] exchange interactions establishes an energy gap that protects the fully symmetric collective manifold, suppressing non-collective excitations, and achieving Heisenberg scaling [MATH] in one to three dimensions for any power-law exponent. We provide an analytical understanding of the mechanism via the analysis of the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum, and demonstrate its effectiveness via numerical simulations of the quantum many-body dynamics. Our findings more broadly apply to other spin-squeezing Hamiltonians, and directly generalize to larger internal spin dimensions. Our results provide a practical pathway towards scalable Heisenberg-limited qudit entanglement generation in experimental platforms such as arrays of (polar) molecules, magnetic atoms, and Rydberg atoms realizing multi-level spin systems.

title: Smp: A General Hyperedge-Based Framework For Circuit-Level Quantum Error Correction
authors: Siying Wang, Yue Yan, Zhixin Xia, Canwei Shi, Hannuo Yuan, Xiang-Bin Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hyperedge faults remain a major challenge in circuit-level quantum error correction. Accurately exploiting hyperedge correlations often requires substantial computational resources, which complicates real-time decoding. Matching-based decoders are fast and scalable, but their pairwise graph representation limits the use of higher-order fault information. Here, we introduce Syndrome Motif Projection (SMP), a general framework for incorporating hyperedge information into matching-based decoding. The key idea is that a hyperedge fault produces a characteristic local syndrome motif. Observing such a motif provides evidence for the corresponding fault. SMP extracts this information directly from the measured syndrome with linear-complexity preprocessing while preserving the matching backend. It can therefore serve as a lightweight front end to existing scalable and real-time matching decoders. We demonstrate SMP across surface code memories, color code memories, and logical gate circuits. On Google's Willow experimental surface code data, SMP improves both standard and correlated matching and outperforms the tested belief matching baseline. For color code memories, SMP combined with Chromobius reduces logical failure probabilities by up to 77.8\%. For logical gate circuits, SMP reduces the failure probability of a six-CNOT circuit by 35.5\% relative to logical observable matching while achieving performance comparable to iterative belief matching. These results demonstrate that SMP provides a lightweight and transferable approach to hyperedge decoding, with a clear path toward integration into scalable real-time decoding architectures for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
tldr: Introduces Syndrome Motif Projection (SMP), a lightweight framework that incorporates hyperedge fault information into matching-based decoders for circuit-level quantum error correction, improving logical failure rates across surface codes, color codes, and gate circuits.
motivation: Hyperedge faults degrade circuit-level quantum error correction, but matching decoders ignore higher-order correlations, while accurately using them is computationally expensive for real-time decoding.
method: SMP extracts characteristic local syndrome motifs produced by hyperedge faults from the measured syndrome with linear-complexity preprocessing and feeds this evidence to existing matching decoders without altering the scalable backend.
result: On Google's Willow surface code data, SMP improves standard and correlated matching and outperforms belief matching; on color codes with Chromobius it reduces logical failure probability by up to 77.8%, and on a six-CNOT logical gate circuit it reduces failure probability by 35.5% relative to logical observable matching while matching iterative belief matching.
conclusion: SMP offers a lightweight, transferable, and scalable approach to hyperedge decoding, with a clear path toward integration into real-time decoders for fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Optimal State Detection Without Likelihood Estimation

abstract: ArXiv:2610.02644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that adaptive Bayesian estimation in fluorescence state detection reduces to a comparison of elapsed time with two arithmetic time sequences fixed by the bright and dark count rates and confidence parameters [MATH] and [MATH]. title: Quantum Error-Corrected Memories Keep Proper Time
authors: Simon J. Devitt Sebastian P. Kish
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02786v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What does quantum error correction do to relativistic proper time? We show that when two error-corrected quantum memories follow distinct worldlines and are controlled by local references, their local correction histories factor exactly from the proper-time difference between them. Error correction therefore does not erase time dilation: when the memories are compared, the accumulated difference appears as a relational phase rotation. During locally referenced operation this rotation is invisible to every local error syndrome; at discrete phases admitted by a code, the final relational evolution instead returns exactly as a deterministic logical gate, including an [MATH]-type Clifford gate at a [MATH] excursion. These results connect fault-tolerant quantum information with relativistic clocks and establish protected quantum memories as a platform for preserving proper-time information and for long-coherence tests of quantum evolution involving relativistic proper time.

method: Analyzes two error-corrected quantum memories with local references, deriving that their local correction histories factor exactly from the proper-time difference between them.
result: The accumulated proper-time difference appears as a relational phase rotation invisible to every local error syndrome, and at discrete code phases it returns as a deterministic logical gate, including a Clifford gate.
conclusion: This connects fault-tolerant quantum information with relativistic clocks and establishes protected quantum memories as a platform for preserving proper-time information and long-coherence tests.

title: From Heat To Homology: Spectral Gap Transfer For Exact Quantum Gibbs Sampling At All Temperatures
authors: Caesnan M. G. Leditto, Kuo-Chin Chen, Min-Hsiu Hsieh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preparing Gibbs states through dissipative dynamics requires controlling convergence for the chosen Hamiltonian [MATH] and coupling operators. However, efficient implementation requires convergence guarantees from the spectral gap of the generator of the dynamics, which remains a crucial challenge. Recent results address the challenge by restricting the dynamics with structural assumptions about the Hamiltonian and its interactions. For the Chen-Kastoryano-Gilyen (CKG) construction and arbitrary finite-dimensional Hamiltonians, we prove an explicit comparison that converts a spectral gap estimate for the infinite-temperature generator into a lower bound on the spectral gap of the CKG quantum Gibbs sampler at every finite positive inverse temperature [MATH]. It allows a single spectral gap estimate at infinite temperature to certify convergence across Hamiltonians and temperatures. Such an estimate is often known from a classical spectral gap estimate, such as the classical random walk spectral gap. For Hodge Laplacians of simplicial complexes as Hamiltonians, we construct coupling operators whose generator at infinite temperature has the same spectral gap as a classical simplicial down-up walk. A positive spectral gap of the walk and bounded spectral width [MATH] give a generator spectral gap independent of the number of simplices at every fixed temperature. We then establish conditions under which the sampler approximately prepares zero-energy (harmonic) states in polynomial evolution time. This provides a conditional convergence guarantee for the state preparation in the thermal approach to quantum topological data analysis.

result: They show that a positive spectral gap of the classical walk and bounded spectral width yield a generator spectral gap independent of the number of simplices at each fixed temperature, and establish conditions under which the sampler approximately prepares harmonic states in polynomial time.
conclusion: This provides a conditional convergence guarantee for exact quantum Gibbs sampling, with implications for the thermal approach to quantum topological data analysis.

title: Counterdiabatic Quantum Circuits
authors: Ankit Wenju Shrestha, Budhaditya Bhattacharjee, Adolfo Del Campo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02312v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Counterdiabatic driving provides a universal route to fast quantum control, but its standard formulation presupposes a Hamiltonian generator. We develop a Hamiltonian-free theory of the adiabatic gauge potential (AGP) for parameter-dependent unitary operators [MATH]. Exact and regularized versions of the AGP follow from a Hermitian, banded linear system at a cost comparable to the Lanczos construction in the Hermitian case, requiring neither diagonalization nor a matrix logarithm. We demonstrate rapid convergence of the truncated Krylov approximation for the kicked top and for an integrable brickwork circuit built from unitary [MATH] matrices, a setting in which no local effective Hamiltonian is available. Our results extend shortcuts to adiabaticity, and AGP-based diagnostics of chaos, to Floquet systems and quantum circuits.
tldr: A Hamiltonian-free theory of the adiabatic gauge potential enables counterdiabatic driving for parameter-dependent unitary operators, extending shortcuts to adiabaticity to Floquet systems and quantum circuits.
motivation: Counterdiabatic driving provides fast quantum control but its standard formulation requires a Hamiltonian generator, limiting its application to Floquet systems and unitary circuits where no local effective Hamiltonian exists.
method: The authors formulate exact and regularized adiabatic gauge potentials for unitary operators via a Hermitian banded linear system, avoiding diagonalization or matrix logarithm, and demonstrate convergence of truncated Krylov approximations for the kicked top and an integrable brickwork circuit of unitary matrices.
result: The approach achieves rapid convergence for both the kicked top and the brickwork circuit, showing that counterdiabatic control can be realized without an explicit Hamiltonian and providing AGP-based chaos diagnostics for Floquet and circuit settings.
conclusion: This work extends shortcuts to adiabaticity and AGP-based chaos diagnostics beyond Hamiltonian systems, opening a route to fast quantum control in Floquet systems and quantum circuits.

title: From Static Lindblad Stabilizability To Robust Physical Control Sequences
authors: Ruifeng Liu Yibin Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dissipative dynamics can stabilize a quantum target without providing a reliable sequence of finite control operations. We derive checkable conditions for implementing such stabilization with imperfect controls, with bounds on convergence, errors during operations, and physical cost. The analysis includes pulses, idle intervals, and all simultaneously acting background dynamics. Using a common Lyapunov measure of deviation from the target, we require a contraction bound that remains uniformly below one over the prescribed uncertainty set after accounting for implementation errors. If all allowed paths preserve the target subspace throughout each operation, repeated cycles converge to that subspace from every initial state, even when errors vary between cycles. Comparison with these certified target-preserving paths gives an explicit long-time error bound under bounded leakage. Two single-qubit counterexamples show why a stabilizing average or a stabilizing generator obtained by unitary conjugation does not ensure these path conditions. The certification approach also supports a finite-library search. For a specified four-level cascade model with finite pulses, calibration and timing errors, dephasing, and bounded pumping, this search yields a sequence with an explicit preparation-time bound. For every initial state, it guarantees trace distance at most [MATH] from the target at the end of preparation and throughout subsequent cycles.
tldr: Derives checkable conditions for robustly stabilizing a target subspace under dissipative Lindblad dynamics with imperfect controls, yielding explicit convergence, error, and preparation-time bounds.
motivation: Static Lindblad stabilizability does not guarantee a reliable finite sequence of control operations when realistic errors, idle intervals, and background dynamics are present.
method: Uses a common Lyapunov measure of deviation from the target and requires a contraction bound uniformly below one over the uncertainty set, accounting for pulses, idle intervals, background dynamics, and implementation errors; also performs a finite-library search.
result: If all allowed paths preserve the target subspace, repeated cycles converge to that subspace from every initial state even with cycle-varying errors; under bounded leakage an explicit long-time error bound follows, and a four-level cascade example yields an explicit preparation-time and trace-distance guarantee.
conclusion: The certification approach provides robust physical control sequences for dissipative stabilization and shows via counterexamples why a stabilizing average or unitarily conjugated generator alone is insufficient, while enabling finite-library search.

title: Investigating Entanglement Dynamics With Dynamical Decoupling Together With Initial Qubit-reservoir Correlations
authors: Rifzah Shahid, Amna Qadeer, Ali Raza Mirza
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the exact entanglement dynamics of two qubits coupled to a common bosonic reservoir through a pure dephasing interaction. We ask how this dynamics changes when the qubits and the reservoir already share correlations before the qubit state is prepared. In that case the system and reservoir first interact for a long time and settle into a joint equilibrium state. Only afterward is the qubit pair projected onto the desired state by a local measurement. For an Ohmic spectral density we obtain the exact reduced two qubit dynamics. Using the Wootters concurrence we show that initial correlations always speed up entanglement sudden death relative to the factorized case, and that this gap grows quadratically with the coupling strength in the weak-to-moderate coupling regime. Finally we show that a symmetric sequence of periodic {\pi} pulses applied to both qubits extends the entanglement lifetime close to a factor of seven over the range of pulse numbers studied.
tldr: The paper studies how initial qubit-reservoir correlations and dynamical decoupling affect the entanglement dynamics of two qubits coupled to a common bosonic dephasing reservoir.

method: They derive exact reduced two-qubit dynamics for an Ohmic spectral density, quantify entanglement via Wootters concurrence, and apply a symmetric sequence of periodic π pulses to both qubits.
result: Initial correlations always speed up entanglement sudden death compared with the factorized case, with the gap growing quadratically with coupling strength, while dynamical decoupling extends entanglement lifetime by up to about a factor of seven.
conclusion: The findings show that initial correlations are detrimental to entanglement preservation in this model, but dynamical decoupling can significantly mitigate the decoherence-induced entanglement loss.

title: Nonreciprocal Coupling Induced Non-Hermitian Entanglement In Optomechanical Systems
authors: W. Y. Hu, H. Yi, H. N. Liu, S. Y. Ge, Cheng Shang, Yan-Hui Zhou, H. Z. Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum entanglement, one of the most intrinsic properties of quantum mechanics, corresponds to a key resource for quantum information. Exceptional points (EPs) are special phase transition points in non-Hermitian systems. Nonreciprocity achieves one-way motion by breaking reciprocal symmetries. However, the connections among quantum entanglement, EPs, and nonreciprocity remain unexplored in non-Hermitian systems. In this paper, we investigate the manipulation of optomechanical entanglement by non-Hermitian coupling between two counter-propagating optical modes based on a whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) resonator coupled with two Rayleigh scatterers. EPs can periodically appear by controlling the relative angle between two nanoparticles. Moreover, the spinning resonator can induce opposite frequency shifts in two counter-propagating optical modes. The logarithmic negativity of entanglement reaches the maximum at EPs, leading to significant enhancement of optomechanical entanglement. In contrast, the entanglement is suppressed at non-EPs but can be recovered by the Sagnac-Fizeau shift. Specially, by driving the resonator at EPs while spinning it at the optimal rotation speed, we achieve switching between classical and quantum nonreciprocity.
tldr: The paper studies how nonreciprocal, non-Hermitian coupling in a whispering-gallery-mode optomechanical resonator can manipulate and enhance optomechanical entanglement at exceptional points.
motivation: Exceptional points and nonreciprocity are well-studied in non-Hermitian physics, but their connection to quantum entanglement in optomechanical systems remained unexplored, motivating a unified treatment of these three phenomena.
method: The authors analyze a WGM resonator coupled to two Rayleigh scatterers, deriving an effective non-Hermitian coupling between counter-propagating optical modes where EPs are tuned by the relative scatterer angle, and compute the logarithmic negativity of the optomechanical entanglement including Sagnac-Fizeau shifts from resonator spinning.
result: Entanglement (logarithmic negativity) is maximized at exceptional points and suppressed away from them, but can be recovered via the Sagnac-Fizeau shift; driving at EPs while spinning at an optimal speed enables switching between classical and quantum nonreciprocity.
conclusion: Nonreciprocal non-Hermitian coupling provides a tunable knob for enhancing and controlling optomechanical entanglement, suggesting EP-based schemes for directional quantum information protocols.

The non-Hermitian coupling between two counter-propagating optical modes is induced by the scatterers, and the relative angle between them controls the appearance of EPs periodically. title: Non-Markovian Entanglement Via Parametrically Mediated Molecular Cavity Optomechanics
authors: Wenyao Hu, H. N. Liu, X. C. Zhang, Cheng Shang, Yan-Hui Zhou, H. Z. Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum entanglement in molecular cavity optomechanical (COM) systems serves as a fundamental resource to explore quantum-enhanced sensing, coherent molecular dynamics, and quantum information processing, which has been studied under Markovian approximation but not yet explored in non-Markovian reservoirs. In this paper, we propose a scheme to manipulate quantum entanglement in molecular COM system coupling with degenerate optical parametric amplifier (DOPA) under Markovian approximation. We reveal that both strength and phase of DOPA can be tuned to enhance optical-vibration entanglement and suppress vibration-vibration entanglement. The optical-vibration entanglement can exist at room temperature, demonstrating strong robustness against thermal noise. Moreover, we extend results from Markovian to non-Markovian regimes, which can further enhance both types of entanglement with DOPA fixed. In particular, we find that non-Markovian effects can reverse influences of DOPA on vibration-vibration entanglement from suppression to enhancement, leading to regeneration of entanglement. The scheme provides an effective way to control and enhance quantum entanglement in molecular COM system through steering DOPA and non-Markovian effects.

method: The authors model a molecular cavity optomechanical system coupled to a DOPA, first under Markovian and then under non-Markovian reservoirs, and tune the DOPA strength and phase to control optical-vibration and vibration-vibration entanglement.
result: DOPA enhances optical-vibration entanglement and suppresses vibration-vibration entanglement at room temperature; non-Markovian effects further enhance both types of entanglement and can reverse the DOPA-induced suppression into enhancement, regenerating entanglement.
conclusion: The scheme provides an effective route to control and enhance entanglement in molecular cavity optomechanical systems by steering the DOPA and exploiting non-Markovian effects, with robustness against thermal noise.

title: Correlated Memory Effect Of Environment In Radical-pair Magnetoreception
authors: Shixuan Chen, Yao Wang, Rui-Xue Xu, Yijing Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the photoreceptor compass model, a light-generated, spin-correlated radical pair undergoes singlet-triplet interconversion driven by Zeeman and anisotropic hyperfine interactions, leading to orientation-dependent reaction yields. In this study, we consider simultaneously the spin environment and the boson environment surrounding the radical-pair system and concentrate on the correlated memory effect of the spin bath. In the linear-response limit, the spin bath is mapped to an effective Gaussian environment. The system dynamics and yields under its influence together with the bosonic bath are propagated uniformly using the hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) or equivalently the dissipaton equations of motion (DEOM) method. The HEOM/DEOM is non-Markovian and non-perturbative, exact for Gaussian environments. Corresponding results of the Markovian Lindblad master equation are also shown for comparison. Numerical demonstrations highlight the non-Markovian memory effect as a crucial ingredient for radical-pair magnetoreception.

method: The radical-pair system is coupled to a spin bath, mapped to an effective Gaussian environment, and to a bosonic bath; dynamics are simulated exactly with hierarchical/dissipaton equations of motion and compared with Markovian Lindblad results.
result: Non-Markovian memory effects from the spin bath significantly modify singlet-triplet interconversion and orientation-dependent reaction yields.
conclusion: Environmental memory is a key ingredient in radical-pair magnetoreception, requiring non-Markovian and non-perturbative treatment.

title: Single-photon Addition To Multimode Quantum Fields At Telecom Wavelengths Using Lithium Niobate And Its Doped Variants

abstract: ArXiv:2610.02473v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimode spectro-temporal non-Gaussian quantum states of light play a crucial role in continuous-variable quantum information processing. In particular, the non-Gaussian quantum states generated through a single-photon addition (SPA) to multimode quantum fields at telecommunication wavelengths constitute a useful resource for quantum technologies. We present a detailed theoretical analysis and numerical simulations of single-photon addition (SPA) and mode-selective single-photon addition (MSSPA) to a multimode quantum field at telecommunication wavelengths. The analysis is performed for congruently grown lithium niobate (LN), [MATH] MgO-doped lithium niobate (MgO:LN) and various concentrations of ZnO-doped lithium niobate (ZnO:LN) bulk crystals. We investigate MSSPA using type-II parametric down-conversion (PDC) and SPA using the type-I PDC processes. We further present spectro-temporal mode-selective SPA at the telecom wavelength using [MATH] MgO:LN for temperatures ranging from [MATH] to [MATH]. In addition, we perform simulations to investigate SPA based on the noncollinear type-I PDC configuration. These theoretical results identify optimal experimental conditions and phase-matching parameters to achieve SPA and mode-selective SPA for LN-based crystals, providing a potential platform for non-Gaussian quantum state engineering at telecommunication wavelengths, mainly at [MATH] nm.

title: Stratification Of The Space Of Density Matrices Via Invariant Theory And Uhlmann's Connection
authors: Howy Jordan, Markus J. Pflaum, Gerd Rudolph
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The space of [MATH] density matrices is the full state space of an [MATH]-level quantum system. While it has been asserted in the literature on quantum information theory that decomposing this state space into equirank pieces yields a Whitney stratification, rigorous proofs have remained absent. Using methods from invariant theory, this work provides a proof that the rank decomposition of the matrix algebra constitutes a (b)-regular stratification in the sense of Whitney. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the Uhlmann connection - which describes the adiabatic holonomy of mixed states and reduces to the Berry connection on pure states - can be geometrically treated as a stratified connection on a stratified vector bundle. Finally, our appendix provides a self-contained exposition of stratified fiber bundles and the new concept of stratified connections, which may be of independent interest.
tldr: This paper proves that the equirank decomposition of the space of density matrices forms a Whitney stratification and interprets the Uhlmann connection as a stratified connection on a stratified fiber bundle.
motivation: Quantum information theory has long assumed that decomposing the state space into equirank pieces yields a Whitney stratification, but rigorous proofs were missing. This work fills that gap and provides a geometric framework for mixed-state holonomy.
method: The authors use invariant theory to prove that the rank decomposition of the matrix algebra is a (b)-regular Whitney stratification. They then recast the Uhlmann connection as a stratified connection on a stratified vector bundle, with a self-contained appendix on stratified fiber bundles and stratified connections.
result: The rank decomposition of density matrices is rigorously shown to be a Whitney stratification. The Uhlmann connection is geometrically treated as a stratified connection, generalizing the Berry connection from pure to mixed states.
conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for the stratification of quantum state space and introduces stratified connections, which may be useful for geometric approaches to mixed-state quantum information.

title: Direct Estimation Of $g^{(2)}(0)$ From Click Statistics Of A Multiplexed Detector

abstract: ArXiv:2610.03040v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present and theoretically analyze a method for direct estimation of the second-order correlation function [MATH] from the click statistics of a multiplexed detector composed of M binary on-off detection channels. We demonstrate the performance of the method for coherent, thermal, amplitude-squeezed, and photon-added coherent states. We also derive a nonclassicality criterion based on the estimated correlation function and show how the method can be adapted to unbalanced detectors. Our work establishes direct estimation of [MATH] as a simple and versatile method for quantitatively characterizing quantum light using multiplexed click detectors.

title: Premonoidal Semantics And Scalable Diagrammatics Of Fermionic Quantum Computing
authors: Titouan Carette Thomas Perez
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local fermionic mode (LFM) based quantum computation has pure state spaces that are isomorphic, via the Jordan-Wigner representation, to qubit state spaces, but its compositional structure is subtly different. Indeed, the algebraic formalism specifying how to embed fermionic systems underlies a notion of parallel composition, for which, in general, the usual interchange law of monoidal categories fails. We give a categorical account of this phenomenon. Starting from the CAR-algebraic semantics of fermionic gate application, we show that LFM processes form a symmetric premonoidal category whose centre is precisely the even, parity-preserving subcategory. The same processes can alternatively be organized with the ordinary tensor product and a fermionic presymmetry that is natural exactly on even maps. To reason diagrammatically in this latter presentation, we introduce pronaps, a relaxation of the notion of prop, in which permutations are not-necessarily-natural, and use them to organize a hierarchy of fragments of the fermionic ZW calculus relevant to the study of fermionic circuits on physically motivated gate-sets. We then extend scalable diagrammatic notation to pronaps. In this setting, syntactic sugars inspired by SZX and GSA are defined, with the specificity that matrix arrows encode minors and determinants, while graph triangles encode pfaffians of principal submatrices. These constructions yield elegant normal forms and completeness proofs for our presentations of the EoW, FoW, EW, and FW fragments. In particular, the FW presentation gives a new normal form for the matchgate fragment, distinct from the rWGS-X normal form of the planar-W (pW) presentation of the same category. The resulting framework connects fermionic circuit semantics, diagrammatic rewriting with scalable notations, and the algebra of determinants and pfaffians.

method: Starting from CAR-algebraic semantics, the authors show that LFM processes form a symmetric premonoidal category whose centre is the even parity-preserving subcategory; they introduce pronaps and extend scalable diagrammatic notations to several fragments of the fermionic ZW calculus.
result: They obtain elegant normal forms and completeness proofs for the EoW, FoW, EW, and FW fragments, with the FW presentation yielding a new normal form for the matchgate fragment that encodes determinants and pfaffians of principal submatrices.
conclusion: The framework connects fermionic circuit semantics, diagrammatic rewriting with scalable notations, and the algebra of determinants and pfaffians, offering a foundation for reasoning about fermionic quantum circuits.

On its own, dense encoding provides a [MATH] improvement over SelectSwap by reducing the leading Toffoli count to [MATH]. Combining it with sequential bit packets gives [MATH], a further halving of the sequential construction's leading cost, and an approximately [MATH] improvement over SelectSwap in the large-[MATH] limit for practical values of [MATH].
tldr: The paper introduces a dense encoding for quantum read-only memory (QROM) that stores two bits of classical information per dirty qubit using both X and Z bases, reducing the leading Toffoli count in fault-tolerant quantum algorithms.
motivation: QROM is a major source of non-Clifford cost in fault-tolerant quantum algorithms, and reducing this cost is especially important in qubit-constrained regimes where table loading dominates the total cost.
method: The dense encoding construction exploits both computational and Hadamard bases to encode two classical bits per dirty qubit, and it is combined with sequential bit packets to further optimize the Toffoli count.
result: Dense encoding alone improves over SelectSwap by reducing the leading Toffoli count, and when combined with sequential bit packets it achieves a further halving, yielding an approximately quadratic improvement over SelectSwap in the large-n limit for practical values.
conclusion: Dense encoding provides a practical and significant reduction in QROM cost for fault-tolerant quantum algorithms, particularly beneficial in resource-constrained settings.

title: Spatiotemporal Quantum Advantages For Rare-event Sampling
authors: Akshat Gupta, Jianjun Chen, Chengran Yang, Mile Gu, Caterina Doglioni, Jayne Thompson, Thomas J. Elliott
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a world fraught with uncertainty, it behooves us to consider the most disastrous possible outcomes, in order that we can best mitigate against them. Often these are extreme risk events -- of high consequence, but low probability. Yet, the rarity of such events limits our ability to study them; there is a paucity of past occurrences to draw upon, and sampling such rare events from models is typically costly in time. Here, we introduce an approach for rare-event sampling based on quantum stochastic models. This integrates the memory advantages of quantum stochastic modelling -- and its associated efficient means of preparing quantum sample states -- with the `speed-ups' of quantum amplitude amplification, to yield simultaneous reductions in spatial and temporal computational complexity compared to classical Monte Carlo-based approaches.
tldr: Introduces quantum rare-event sampling using quantum stochastic models and amplitude amplification to reduce spatial and temporal complexity versus classical Monte Carlo.
motivation: Rare high-consequence events are difficult to study because they are low-probability and costly to sample from classical models.
method: Combines the memory advantages of quantum stochastic modelling and efficient quantum sample-state preparation with quantum amplitude amplification.
result: Achieves simultaneous reductions in spatial and temporal computational complexity compared to classical Monte Carlo-based rare-event sampling.
conclusion: Quantum stochastic models with amplitude amplification can provide spatiotemporal advantages for rare-event sampling, though the work sits outside the core information-theoretic focus areas.

title: The Complexity Of Entangled Graph Colouring Via Polymorphisms
authors: Eric Culf
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) with operator assignments to the variables provide a well-structured setting to study the decision complexity of the entangled value of classes of nonlocal games. Due to the CSP dichotomy theorem, the complexity of constraint satisfaction problems with classical assignments can be fully understood by studying the symmetries of the CSP, in terms of the polymorphisms of the underlying relational structure. In this work, we show that the polymorphism-based reductions between CSPs can be generalised to gap-preserving reductions between entangled CSPs based on an entangled analogue of the polymorphisms. This reduction allows us to show undecidability of entangled graph colouring with more than three colours, a problem that has proved resistant to prior hardness reductions based on commutativity gadgets.
tldr: The paper generalizes polymorphism-based reductions to entangled CSPs via entangled polymorphisms and proves undecidability of entangled graph colouring with more than three colours.
motivation: The decision complexity of the entangled value of nonlocal games and CSPs is a central problem, and previous hardness reductions based on commutativity gadgets have failed for entangled graph colouring.
method: An entangled analogue of polymorphisms is introduced to build gap-preserving reductions between entangled CSPs, extending the classical polymorphism-based reduction framework.
result: The reduction proves undecidability of entangled graph colouring for more than three colours, resolving a case resistant to prior hardness techniques.
conclusion: Polymorphism-based reductions provide a powerful tool for studying the complexity of entangled CSPs and nonlocal games.

title: When Normalization Selects The Sign: Auditing Robustness Ablations In Quantum Attention
authors: Owen Friedewald, Srikar Alla, Ali Shiri Sichani, Chi-Ren Shyu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Removing an input-scaling module changes both a classifier and the perturbations reaching its encoder. A robustness difference can therefore reflect the comparison rule as well as the module. We demonstrate this problem in a four-qubit quantum-attention detector on generated power-grid trajectories. A learned scaling module appears beneficial at a fixed physical attack budget, but matching an upper bound on perturbations at the encoder reverses the ordering. Neither comparison alone establishes a robustness benefit caused by the module. The initial test also perturbs clean examples into attacked examples while retaining their original labels; tests restricted to already attacked examples do not establish a benefit. Replacing a trained model's input scales disrupts detection. Retraining its linear classification layer restores the detection rate, but changes individual predictions, leaving the comparison descriptive rather than causal. Two further design checks explain why the input quantum Fisher information regularizer cannot train this model's query parameters, and why removing confidence bounds does not establish a larger certified radius. The evidence is limited to ten seeds, exact simulation, synthetic data, and a restricted set of attacks; classical baselines achieve better clean prediction. The practical lesson is to specify which perturbation budget is fixed, check that attacks preserve labels and interventions preserve predictions, and distinguish exploratory controls from confirmatory evidence.
tldr: The paper audits robustness ablations in a four-qubit quantum attention detector, revealing that comparisons can reverse depending on whether a physical attack budget or an encoder perturbation bound is fixed.
motivation: Removing an input-scaling module changes both the classifier and the perturbations reaching its encoder, so a robustness difference may reflect the comparison rule rather than the module's causal effect.
method: They train a quantum-attention model on synthetic power-grid trajectories, compare robustness under a fixed physical attack budget versus a matched encoder perturbation bound, and perform further checks including retraining the linear classification layer.
result: The apparent benefit of the scaling module reverses when matching perturbation bounds; retraining restores detection rate but changes individual predictions; the input quantum Fisher information regularizer cannot train query parameters, and removing confidence bounds does not enlarge the certified radius.
conclusion: Robustness audits must specify which perturbation budget is fixed, ensure attacks preserve labels and interventions preserve predictions, and distinguish exploratory from confirmatory evidence.

title: Conditional Correctness In List Decoding: How A Late Second Codeword Can Rescue Confidence In The First
authors: Conrad Struss, Muriel Medard, Ken R. Duffy
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In error correction, the difference between a codeword and a received word, a candidate noise sequence, carries information on the confidence of the codeword as a proposed decoding. For additive channels, it is known that if noise sequences are ranked in decreasing order of likelihood, a lower rank correlates with higher confidence in a decoding. Here we substantially expand considerations by exploring the relationship between the likelihood ranks arising in list decoding and the posterior probability of decoding correctness, establishing that the ranks associated with subsequent list entries carry reliability information that is not obtainable from the first rank alone. Building on the recent development of Soft-Output Guessing Random Additive Noise Decoding, we first show that, under a random codebook model, soft-output expressions for list decoding coincide with the exact finite-blocklength conditional probabilities of decoding correctness. For hard-decision maximum likelihood decoding, we characterize the asymptotic reliability of the first list entry. We identify a decision function whose sign determines whether the posterior correctness probability of the first entry in the list converges to one or zero and whose absolute value gives the exponential rate of convergence. Perhaps surprisingly, the asymptotic reliability of the first list entry depends only on the first, second and last ranks. For list size one, the result recovers the previously known likelihood-rank threshold for reliable decoding. For list size two, a sufficiently late second entry can imply that the first entry is asymptotically correct even when its rank, viewed in isolation, would indicate otherwise.
tldr: The paper analyzes how likelihood ranks from list decoding relate to the posterior probability of decoding correctness, showing that a sufficiently late second list entry can imply the first entry is asymptotically correct.
motivation: In error correction, the noise-sequence rank relative to a received word is known to indicate decoding confidence, but the reliability information carried by subsequent list-decoding entries has been unexplored.
method: Using soft-output Guessing Random Additive Noise Decoding (GRAND) under a random codebook model, the authors derive exact finite-blocklength conditional probabilities of decoding correctness for list decoding and characterize the asymptotic reliability of the first list entry via a decision function depending only on the first, second and last ranks.
result: Soft-output list-decoding expressions match exact correctness probabilities, and the asymptotic reliability of the first entry is governed by the first, second, and last likelihood ranks, with a late second entry sometimes rescuing the first entry's correctness.
conclusion: List-decoding ranks beyond the first carry genuine reliability information, generalizing the known likelihood-rank threshold (list size one) and providing a new criterion for asymptotic decoding confidence.

title: Bias-Corrected Estimators For Joint Entropy, Conditional Entropy, And Mutual Information In The Discrete Bivariate Case: Theory And An Application To Motor Insurance
authors: Amadou Diadie Ba
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the finite-sample bias of plug-in estimators for joint entropy, conditional entropy, and mutual information for finitely supported discrete random variables. Using the univariate reduction framework developed in our companion works, we derive explicit first-order bias formulas. For a pair (X,Y) with support sizes r and s, the biases are respectively -(rs-1)/(2n), -r(s-1)/(2n), and (r-1)(s-1)/(2n). We then propose bias-corrected estimators for the three measures and prove that the uncorrected and corrected versions are asymptotically equivalent, differing by a deterministic term of order O(1/n); consequently, they share the same asymptotic distribution. A simulation study validates the theoretical results, including a dedicated independence study and the relationship with Wilks' theorem. An application to a motor insurance portfolio, where X is the driver's age class and Y the claim severity class, illustrates the improvement brought by the bias correction for risk classification.
tldr: The paper derives first-order finite-sample bias corrections for plug-in estimators of joint entropy, conditional entropy, and mutual information in discrete bivariate settings, with an application to motor insurance risk classification.
motivation: Plug-in entropy estimators suffer from finite-sample bias, especially for small samples and large support sizes, which can mislead downstream analyses.
method: Using a univariate reduction framework, the authors derive explicit first-order bias formulas and propose bias-corrected estimators, validated by simulations and an insurance application.
result: The biases are -(rs-1)/(2n), -r(s-1)/(2n), and (r-1)(s-1)/(2n); corrected and uncorrected estimators are asymptotically equivalent and share the same asymptotic distribution.
conclusion: Bias correction improves finite-sample estimation of discrete information measures, but the work is purely classical and does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: The Coverage Depth Problem In Distributed Dna Data Storage
authors: Xiangliang Kong, Ohad Elishco, Chen Wang, Tolga M. Duman
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random sampling in DNA sequencing produces repeated reads, increasing retrieval latency and sequencing cost. We study the coverage-depth problem for full-message recovery in distributed DNA storage under noiseless uniform sampling, where strands are partitioned among [MATH] containers and one strand is independently sampled with replacement from each container per round. For arbitrary linear codes and ordered partitions, we derive exact formulas for the recovery-time distribution and expectation. We prove that MDS codes, whenever they exist, are optimal for every fixed partition, and establish a universal lower bound on the expected total read cost together with its equality conditions. For MDS codes, we identify container-size regimes that yield genuine savings in total reads and regimes that provide only parallelism without changing the asymptotic sequencing cost. For simplex codes, we prove that the [MATH]-ary simplex code is, up to isomorphism, the unique single-container minimizer among codes with the same parameters, resolving a recent conjecture by Bertuzzo, Ravagnani, and Yaakobi. We further construct a partition attaining the minimum total read cost and derive bounds for intermediate and balanced partitions. These results clarify when distributed sampling reduces latency alone and when it also reduces sequencing cost.
tldr: This paper studies the coverage-depth problem in distributed DNA data storage, deriving exact recovery-time distributions and optimal coding strategies for full-message recovery under random sampling.
motivation: Random sampling in DNA sequencing leads to repeated reads, increasing retrieval latency and sequencing cost, so it is important to understand how distributed storage and coding affect coverage depth and total read cost.
method: The authors model strands partitioned among multiple containers, with one strand sampled with replacement per container each round, and analyze linear codes, MDS codes, and simplex codes for recovery-time distribution and expected total read cost.
result: They prove MDS codes are optimal for any fixed partition, establish a universal lower bound on expected total read cost, identify regimes where distributed sampling reduces cost versus only latency, and show that the q-ary simplex code is the unique single-container minimizer, resolving a recent conjecture.
conclusion: The work clarifies when distributed sampling reduces latency alone and when it also reduces sequencing cost, providing theoretical foundations for coding design in distributed DNA data storage.

title: Low-Density Parity-Check Codes Of High Girth From Permutation Polynomials
authors: Tasawwar Hussain, Anthony G\'omez-Fonseca, Tefjol Pllaha
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check (QC-LDPC) codes are widely used in modern communication standards due to their simple structure and efficient encoder and decoder implementations. However, the commutativity of the circulant permutation matrices used in their construction significantly limits their girth and minimum distance, affecting iterative decoding performance. In this paper, we investigate protograph-based codes constructed using permutation polynomials of higher degree, focusing on a closed family of non-commuting binomial permutation polynomials that enables these constructions to exceed both of these girth and minimum distance upper bounds while maintaining a simple representation. Simulation results demonstrate improved decoding performance compared to constructions based on affine permutation polynomials, which include QC-LDPC codes.
tldr: Constructs protograph-based LDPC codes using high-degree permutation polynomials to exceed girth and minimum distance limits of quasi-cyclic LDPC codes.
motivation: The commutativity of circulant permutation matrices in QC-LDPC codes limits girth and minimum distance, degrading iterative decoding performance.
method: Investigates protograph-based codes built from a closed family of non-commuting binomial permutation polynomials of higher degree.
result: The proposed constructions surpass both girth and minimum distance upper bounds while retaining a simple representation, and simulations show improved decoding over affine permutation polynomial constructions.
conclusion: Higher-degree permutation polynomials enable classical LDPC codes with better girth and distance than QC-LDPC, but the work is purely classical coding theory without quantum extension.

title: SoK: Stablecoins In The Quantum Era
authors: Panagiotis Chatzigiannis, Navid Alamati, Suvradip Chakraborty, Duc V. Le
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stablecoins support payments, trading, collateral, and cross-chain settlement across the digital-asset ecosystem. They also concentrate value behind issuer, custody, upgrade, oracle, and bridge keys while inheriting the quantum vulnerabilities of host-chain accounts, consensus, rollups, and privacy systems. This paper presents a Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on post-quantum stablecoins.
