motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as agents that act on behalf of users through interfaces that pre-fill suggested values, yet it is unclear whether models treat such defaults as purely informational or as suggestions that systematically bias their decisions.
method: The authors measure default deference in a common-pool resource extraction game and a threshold public-good contribution game, quantifying how pre-filled defaults shift each model's choice distribution relative to a no-default baseline across varying default values, wordings, and action-space granularities.
result: Defaults pull probability mass toward the default value in both games, but the magnitude depends strongly on wording (permission-style wording reduces pull, more so in CPR than TPG), is weaker in coarse action spaces, and is larger for conflict defaults than agreement defaults.
conclusion: Default deference in LLMs depends jointly on the model, the wording of the interface, and the structure of available choices, implying that evaluations of agentic systems must control for the surrounding choice architecture to avoid missing a key source of behavioural variation.

title: Persona Guardrail: A Production-Grade Defense Framework For Agentic Systems
authors: Bijeeta Pal, Sridhar Reddy Maddireddy, Muhaimin Bin Munir, Zoltan Puha, Max Zhurovich, Adi Raghavendra, Sean Tout
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model-based agents are increasingly deployed to perform domain-specific tasks by interacting with enterprise knowledge, tools, and external services. Existing runtime guardrails primarily target prompt injection and other attack-specific behaviors under a black-box threat model, but provide limited guarantees that agents operate within their intended functionality. As a result, production agents remain vulnerable to malicious requests and out-of-domain queries that existing defenses often fail to distinguish. We present Persona Guardrail, a production-grade runtime defense framework that enforces explicit functional boundaries for customer-facing agentic AI systems through synchronous input and output validation driven by semantic allowlist and blocklist specifications. We also introduce PAGE (Persona-Aware Guardrail Evaluation), a benchmark for evaluating function-specific guardrails across benign, adversarial, and out-of-domain interactions on both user and agent turns. Compared with a generic LLM-based guardrail, Persona Guardrail improves overall accuracy from 85.7% to 95.9%, increases out-of-domain detection from 57.3% to 93.5%, and reduces the false-approved rate from 25.0% to 4.7%. Currently deployed in production, Persona Guardrail meets its latency budget while sustaining a very low false-block and false-allow rate under realistic production workloads. These results demonstrate that Persona Guardrail provides a practical, scalable, and production-ready foundation for securing agentic AI systems.
tldr: Persona Guardrail is a production-grade runtime defense framework that enforces functional boundaries for customer-facing LLM agents via semantic allowlist and blocklist validation.
motivation: Existing runtime guardrails focus on prompt injection and attack-specific behaviors under black-box threat models, leaving production agents vulnerable to malicious requests and out-of-domain queries that are often indistinguishable from benign interactions.
method: The framework performs synchronous input and output validation using semantic allowlist and blocklist specifications, and introduces the PAGE benchmark to evaluate function-specific guardrails across benign, adversarial, and out-of-domain interactions on both user and agent turns.
result: Compared with a generic LLM-based guardrail, Persona Guardrail improves overall accuracy from 85.7% to 95.9%, raises out-of-domain detection from 57.3% to 93.5%, and reduces the false-approved rate from 25.0% to 4.7%, while meeting production latency budgets.
conclusion: Persona Guardrail offers a practical, scalable, and production-ready foundation for securing agentic AI systems by explicitly enforcing intended functional boundaries.

title: CorrectGuard: Eyes-Off Correctness Estimation For Black-Box Security Guardrails
authors: Adam Faulkner, Nil-Jana Akpinar, Matthew Dressman
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI services increasingly rely on black-box security guardrails, yet privacy-preserving model auditing regimes often cannot measure how well these systems perform in both a human eyes-off production setting, which disallows human inspection of user input, and a machine eyes-off setting, which disallows model inspection of such input. We introduce CorrectGuard, an eyes-off correctness estimation framework for both settings, which involves an independent model-based evaluator predicting whether guardrail decisions on human- and machine-inaccessible inputs are correct using only labeled eyes-on data and without access to the guardrail's internals. We evaluate in-context learning, embedding, and finetuning-based correctness models under leave-one-dataset-out evaluation across 13 safety and security datasets spanning harmful content, jailbreaks, prompt injection, and extraction, and across open-weight guardrails treated uniformly as black boxes. Across both human and machine eyes-off settings (the latter implemented using privacy-preserving fingerprinting of inputs), in-context-learning-based correctness classifiers substantially improve error identification across guardrails, achieving up to a 25 percentage-point increase in macro accuracy, as do finetuning-based approaches which provide a nearly 15-point boost, although performance varies sharply across guardrails and held-out datasets. Correctness scores also support guardrail decision ranking and abstention: across 3 guardrails, the best correctness rankings reduce AURC from unranked baselines of 0.33-0.44 to 0.17-0.22, while the best operating points retain 37.5-52.0% of guardrail decisions at 15% observed risk. These results show that external correctness models can expose systematic failures and support guardrail decision abstention without privileged access to the guardrail.
tldr: CorrectGuard is a framework that estimates the correctness of black-box AI security guardrail decisions without human or model inspection of the input, using external correctness models trained on labeled eyes-on data.
motivation: Privacy-preserving auditing regimes forbid human inspection (eyes-off) or model inspection (machine eyes-off) of user inputs, leaving no way to measure how well black-box security guardrails actually perform in production.
method: Independent evaluator models based on in-context learning, embeddings, and finetuning predict whether guardrail decisions on inaccessible inputs are correct, evaluated under leave-one-dataset-out across 13 safety datasets and several open-weight guardrails treated as black boxes.
result: In-context-learning correctness classifiers improve macro accuracy by up to 25 percentage points and finetuning by nearly 15 points, and correctness scores enable decision ranking (AURC 0.33-0.44 to 0.17-0.22) and abstention retaining 37.5-52.0% of decisions at 15% observed risk.
conclusion: External correctness models can expose systematic guardrail failures and support abstention without privileged access, but performance varies sharply across guardrails and held-out datasets.

title: A Secure dToF LiDAR SoC With Dual-Domain Fingerprinting And Event-Driven Afe Circuit Achieving Sensor-Level Attack Resilience
authors: Risa Nonaka, Ryoya Matsuno, Shota Nagai, Satomi Miyagi, Yuki Hayakawa, Ryo Suzuki, Kazuma Ikeda, Ozora Sako, Rokuto Nagata, Ryo Yoshida, Shimpei Ando, Wenlun Zhang, Kentaro Yoshioka
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03562v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent studies have shown that most commercial direct time-of-flight (dToF) LiDARs can be spoofed by injecting high-frequency laser pulses into the receiver, which can erase pedestrians from the point cloud. This paper presents the first dToF LiDAR system-on-chip (SoC) with integrated sensor-level hardware security against spoofing attacks. We propose Dual-Domain Fingerprinting (DDF), which emits laser pulse pairs whose time interval and amplitude ratio are both randomized and authenticates received echoes in this two-dimensional space, so that spoofed signals are rejected before they corrupt the ranging result. An Event-Driven AFE (ED-AFE) activates the ADC only around pulse peaks: it digitizes three samples around each peak with a triggered ADC at 1-GHz sampling and applies parabolic interpolation, achieving 1-cm distance resolution with a 99% reduction in ADC power. A time-modulated laser driver controls the laser amplitude from 10% to 100% by modulating the charge time of a laser capacitor, providing the microsecond-order amplitude modulation required by DDF. A LiDAR system with a 16-channel 65-nm CMOS prototype SoC demonstrates up to 120-m ranging and an AFE power of 3.1 mW per channel, 60% lower than prior art. In a proof-of-concept experiment in which the dual-domain authentication is applied to measured sensor data, 73% of the point cloud is protected under spoofing attack, compared with 0% without DDF.
tldr: A direct time-of-flight LiDAR system-on-chip with dual-domain fingerprinting and an event-driven AFE circuit that resists spoofing attacks at the sensor level.
motivation: Commercial dToF LiDARs are vulnerable to spoofing via injected high-frequency laser pulses, which can erase pedestrians from point clouds and compromise safety-critical applications.
method: The chip emits randomized laser pulse pairs and authenticates echoes in a two-dimensional interval-amplitude space, while an event-driven AFE digitizes only around pulse peaks to reduce power.
result: The 16-channel 65-nm CMOS prototype achieves up to 120-m ranging with 3.1 mW per channel AFE power, and protects 73% of the point cloud under spoofing versus 0% without the defense.
conclusion: Integrated sensor-level hardware security can substantially improve LiDAR resilience to spoofing while maintaining low power and high distance resolution.

title: Professional Perspectives On Community And Public Engagement With Fusion Energy
authors: Jared Owens, Shanna R. Daly, Porter Malcolm, Aditi Verma
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fusion energy technology is rapidly approaching demonstrator deployment, but relatively little consideration has been given to publics' perceptions of or engagement with the technology. This research explores the perspectives of diverse professionals involved with the US fusion energy industry as to their knowledge on, valuation of, and preparedness for community and public (C&P) engagement on fusion energy. Participants perceived multifaceted value in C&P engagement from both industry and personal perspectives including an expressed desire for self-involvement in engagement activities, though ideally with increased support from home organizations and from engagement experts. Participants also revealed framings of fusion C&P engagement that align with deficit and contextual models of science communication thinking. These findings suggest an opportunity for collaboration between fusion professionals and engagement experts beyond one-way science communication to more participatory engagements with implications for the future of fusion energy.
tldr: This paper examines how professionals in the US fusion energy industry perceive and value community and public engagement, revealing framings that align with deficit and contextual models of science communication.
motivation: Fusion energy technology is approaching demonstrator deployment, yet public perceptions of and engagement with fusion have received relatively little attention.
method: The study explores perspectives of diverse professionals involved in the US fusion energy industry through qualitative analysis of their knowledge, valuation, and preparedness for community and public engagement.
result: Participants saw multifaceted value in engagement, expressed a desire for self-involvement ideally with more support from home organizations and engagement experts, and revealed science communication framings consistent with deficit and contextual models.
conclusion: The findings suggest an opportunity for collaboration between fusion professionals and engagement experts to move beyond one-way communication toward more participatory public engagement.

title: The Geometry Of Monarch Matrix Approximation
authors: Shintaro Yoshizawa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Helmke and Shayman showed that, for generic targets, least-squares distance to the manifold of rank-r matrices is a nondegenerate Morse function whose indices are governed by Bruhat-cell codimensions. We develop the analogous theory for Monarch matrices, products of a fixed permutation matrix with two block-diagonal factors. The parametrization's gauge dimension, as well as the codimensions and closure relations of the associated Bruhat-type cells, is determined by a common transfer-matrix invariant, although these quantities are generally distinct. In the equal-block case, we prove the Monarch-Schur theorem, characterizing the permutations that minimize gauge freedom and maximize manifold dimension, and derive a general lower bound for arbitrary partitions. We further establish generic second-order nondegeneracy, a Morse-index formula, and an explicit focal set of measure zero. Finally, we show that the unregularized gradient flow lacks coercivity because of unbounded flat directions. A quartic regularizer restores global convergence, selects a canonical minimum-norm exact solution when one exists, and otherwise yields a well-defined best-approximation image. The regularizer preserves the Monarch architecture and provides a geometric interpretation of weight decay in structured factorized layers.
tldr: Develops a geometric theory of Monarch matrix approximation, covering gauge dimension, Bruhat-type cells, Morse theory, and regularized gradient flow for structured factorized layers.
motivation: Understanding the geometry and optimization landscape of Monarch matrices is important for structured matrix approximation and factorized neural network layers.
method: Uses transfer-matrix invariants, Bruhat-cell codimensions and closure relations, Morse-index formulas, second-order nondegeneracy, and a quartic regularizer to analyze approximation and gradient flow.
result: Proves the Monarch-Schur theorem, derives a lower bound for arbitrary partitions, establishes generic second-order nondegeneracy and an explicit focal set, and shows that unregularized gradient flow lacks coercivity while a quartic regularizer restores global convergence.
conclusion: Provides a geometric interpretation of weight decay in Monarch-style factorized layers and identifies canonical minimum-norm or best-approximation solutions.

title: Learning Closure Of Dynamical Systems With Kernel Ridge Regression
authors: Evan Habbershaw, John Harlim, Senwei Liang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a closure modeling framework for identifying missing components of dynamical systems using Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR). The framework addresses two classes of closure problems: difference-equation closures arising in ODE and PDE settings, and algebraic closures arising from moment closure in kinetic equations. For the first class, we derive an error bound in an ODE setting that quantifies contributions from time integration, approximation of unresolved scales, and interpolation required to couple unresolved-scale effects to the resolved solver. Numerical experiments on the Lorenz-63 system and the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation demonstrate accurate long-horizon predictions and substantial improvements over an LSTM-based closure model. For the second class, we consider moment closure for a one-dimensional kinetic equation by modeling discrepancies between kinetic and macroscopic fluxes as a function of the resolved macroscopic variables. We compare global KRR models based on PCA coordinates with spatially local models. While the global model performs well for unimodal initial conditions, its accuracy deteriorates for bimodal initial conditions. Spatially local models with appropriate modeling inputs improve robustness and achieve higher predictive accuracy.
tldr: The paper develops a Kernel Ridge Regression framework for learning closure models of dynamical systems, addressing both ODE/PDE difference-equation closures and kinetic moment closures.
motivation: Closure modeling is necessary to capture unresolved-scale effects in reduced-order simulations of multiscale dynamical systems, where missing terms can degrade long-term predictive accuracy.
method: The authors derive an error bound for KRR-based difference-equation closures and apply KRR to model discrepancies in moment closure, comparing global PCA-based models with spatially local models.
result: Numerical experiments on the Lorenz-63 system and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation show accurate long-horizon predictions and improvements over an LSTM closure; for kinetic moment closure, global KRR works for unimodal initial conditions but deteriorates for bimodal ones, while local models are more robust.
conclusion: KRR provides an effective closure modeling framework, with spatially local models improving predictive accuracy and robustness for more complex initial conditions.

title: Control Of Markov Jump Linear Systems With Uncertain Lumpable Cluster Observations
authors: Carlos A. F. Persiani, Ram Padmanabhan, Melkior Ornik, Marco H. Terra
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we consider the control of Markov jump linear systems when the active system mode is not exactly known. We rather assume that this true mode is only known to belong to an observed cluster of modes, making both the dynamics and the associated transition probabilities uncertain. We construct a min-max optimal control problem in this setting, with the objective of robust regulation. Using results in regularized least mean-square optimization, we describe how the solution of this problem can be reduced to a Riccati recursion, such that the controller depends only on knowledge of which cluster the mode lies in. We subsequently establish convergence of the recursion and stability of the resulting closed-loop system. A numerical example illustrates the effectiveness of the proposed methodology.
tldr: The paper develops robust min-max optimal control for Markov jump linear systems when the active mode is only known to belong to an observed cluster, reducing the solution to a Riccati recursion.
motivation: In Markov jump linear systems, the true active mode is often not exactly known, making dynamics and transition probabilities uncertain, so robust regulation methods are needed.
method: The authors formulate a min-max optimal control problem under cluster observation uncertainty and use regularized least mean-square optimization to reduce it to a Riccati recursion whose controller depends only on the observed cluster.
result: They establish convergence of the Riccati recursion and stability of the resulting closed-loop system, and illustrate the approach with a numerical example.
conclusion: The proposed cluster-based controller provides an effective robust regulation strategy for Markov jump linear systems with uncertain mode observations.

title: High-Dimensional Regularization Of The Spatial Sign Covariance Matrix For Robust Shape Estimation
authors: Jonas Elmerraji, James C. Spall, Mateo D\'iaz
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Covariance estimation is a key component of many applications in system identification and data-driven control. Although heavy-tailed distributions may lack a covariance matrix to estimate, the shape matrix provides a well-defined, scale-free generalization for the broad family of elliptical distributions. In this setting, practitioners often employ Tyler's M-estimator (TME), which is defined implicitly and is computed using a fixed-point iteration. The spatial sign covariance matrix estimator (SSCM) offers a much simpler alternative: it corresponds to one iteration of TME. Yet, the SSCM has been largely regarded as an inferior estimator due to its statistical inconsistency under fixed-dimensional asymptotics. By contrast, using second-order tools from random matrix theory, we establish that, under standard assumptions, SSCM asymptotically dominates TME in Frobenius risk when dimension and sample size grow proportionally. This advantage arises from implicit regularization, which reduces variance at the cost of a bias that vanishes as the dimension grows. Numerical experiments support the theoretical predictions even at moderate dimensions.
tldr: This paper studies high-dimensional regularization of the spatial sign covariance matrix (SSCM) and shows it asymptotically dominates Tyler's M-estimator in Frobenius risk under proportional growth.
motivation: Robust shape estimation is important for heavy-tailed elliptical distributions where covariance may not exist, and the SSCM is simpler than Tyler's M-estimator but previously thought inferior due to inconsistency in fixed dimensions.
method: Using second-order random matrix theory tools, the authors analyze the asymptotic Frobenius risk of SSCM and TME when dimension and sample size grow proportionally, supported by numerical experiments.
result: SSCM asymptotically dominates TME in Frobenius risk under standard assumptions, with implicit regularization reducing variance at the cost of a bias that vanishes as dimension increases.
conclusion: The SSCM, despite being a single iteration of TME, can be preferable in high-dimensional regimes, challenging its conventional inferiority and providing theoretical justification.

title: A Hybrid CNN-adjoint Optimization Framework For Reconstruction Of Viscoelastic Tissue Properties In Magnetic Resonance Elastography
authors: Anwesa Dey, Johann Rudi, Elena Cherkaev
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02634v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) is a noninvasive imaging modality for quantifying the viscoelastic properties of soft tissues from shear wave propagation. Recovering the complex-valued shear modulus from measured displacement fields leads to a severely ill-posed inverse problem, particularly in the presence of noise and limited boundary excitations. We investigate adjoint-based optimization, convolutional neural network (CNN) reconstruction, and a hybrid framework combining both approaches. The forward model is based on a scalar form of the modified stationary Stokes system with a complex shear modulus. We establish well-posedness of the forward problem, existence of minimizers, and first-order optimality conditions for the adjoint-based formulation, and implement a nonlinear conjugate-gradient method with Armijo line search. While PDE-constrained optimization can accurately refine coefficient reconstructions, its performance depends strongly on initialization. We therefore construct a two-dimensional CNN that maps complex-valued displacement measurements to spatially varying complex shear modulus fields and provides rapid, informative initial reconstructions. The proposed hybrid method uses the CNN reconstruction to initialize the adjoint-based optimization, yielding faster convergence and improved accuracy. The CNN is trained on coefficient fields containing individual perturbations and tested on both individual and previously unseen combined configurations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the CNN generalizes to these more challenging configurations, while subsequent PDE-constrained optimization further refines the reconstructed coefficient. These results demonstrate the potential of combining data-driven initialization with physics-based optimization for efficient and accurate MRE reconstruction.
tldr: The paper develops a hybrid CNN-adjoint optimization framework for reconstructing viscoelastic tissue properties in magnetic resonance elastography, combining deep learning initialization with PDE-constrained optimization.
motivation: MRE reconstruction of complex shear modulus is severely ill-posed, and adjoint-based optimization depends strongly on initialization while pure CNN reconstruction may lack physical accuracy.
method: The authors formulate a scalar modified stationary Stokes forward model, prove well-posedness and existence of minimizers, implement nonlinear conjugate-gradient adjoint optimization, and train a 2D CNN to map complex displacement fields to initial complex shear modulus estimates.
result: Numerical experiments show the CNN generalizes to unseen combined perturbation configurations and the hybrid method achieves faster convergence and improved accuracy over adjoint-only optimization.
conclusion: Combining data-driven initialization with physics-based optimization is promising for efficient and accurate MRE tissue property reconstruction.

title: Higher-Order Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks For Dynamics
authors: Jeremie Fish Kevin Slote
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ability to derive the governing equations of a dynamical system from data is essential for prediction and control across many scientific fields. Two challenges, however, are the expansion of candidate terms when reducing higher-order equations to first-order form and noise from estimating derivatives. We propose Higher-Order-KANDy, which addresses both problems by using delay and derivative ("jet") embeddings of the original data with derivative-ordered Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Dynamics (KANDy) layers stacked into a machine learning architecture. Compared with SINDy and WSINDy on noisy data, Higher-Order-KANDy learns governing equations without a candidate library (e.g., recovering the full-period [MATH] with nothing named in advance), natively for higher-order systems, and holds the correct term structure as noise grows, selecting the exact active set on every seed at noise levels up to 7.5% where an oracle weak-form regression admits a spurious term, though the oracle remains the more accurate coefficient estimator. We leverage the relationship between delay and differential embeddings, along with the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, to construct a delay-to-jet map and learn it as a Kolmogorov-Arnold network to preserve derivative structure and provide meaningful terms that appear in the governing equation. In our synthetic benchmarks, this construction recovers equations in the presence of coarse sampling and noise.
tldr: Higher-Order-KANDy uses delay and derivative embeddings with derivative-ordered Kolmogorov-Arnold Network layers to discover governing equations of higher-order dynamical systems from noisy data without a candidate library.
motivation: Deriving governing equations from data is essential for prediction and control, but higher-order systems suffer from candidate-term explosion when reduced to first order and from noise in derivative estimation.
method: The authors construct a delay-to-jet map using the relationship between delay and differential embeddings, learn it as a Kolmogorov-Arnold network, and stack derivative-ordered KANDy layers to preserve derivative structure.
result: On synthetic benchmarks, Higher-Order-KANDy recovers equations under coarse sampling and noise, selects the exact active set up to 7.5% noise on every seed where an oracle weak-form regression admits a spurious term, though the oracle estimates coefficients more accurately.
conclusion: Higher-Order-KANDy enables library-free, native higher-order equation discovery that is robust to noise, leveraging KANs to maintain meaningful derivative terms in the recovered dynamics.

title: Input-Endpoint Compactness And Essential Norms For Weighted Bilinear Hardy Operators
authors: Saikat Kanjilal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study compactness of the product of two weighted Hardy primitives into [MATH], [MATH], on the input boundary [MATH], where at least one input exponent is [MATH] or [MATH]. For [MATH], [MATH], boundedness implies compactness when [MATH]. For [MATH], the corresponding range is [MATH]. At and above these boundaries compactness is characterized by additional active-tail decay, and critical power weights give bounded noncompact examples. The endpoint reductions use cumulative Stieltjes measures with their initial atoms and strict Hardy-Copson brackets. An output-mass allocation argument proves local finite-rank density, including quasi-Banach targets. Applying the localization principles developed for the interior-input regime identifies the essential distance, finite-rank distance and Hausdorff noncompactness radius with the coupled active tail, with the appropriate metric power when [MATH]. For a finite left endpoint, ordinary [MATH] inputs admit an exact scalar transfer completed by linear nodal approximation.
tldr: This paper studies compactness and essential norms of weighted bilinear Hardy operators on input endpoints, using Stieltjes measures and localization arguments.
motivation: The work aims to characterize compactness and essential norm behavior for multilinear Hardy-type operators near endpoint exponents, extending boundedness-to-compactness principles and identifying noncompact critical cases.
method: The authors use cumulative Stieltjes measures, Hardy-Copson brackets, output-mass allocation arguments, and localization principles to prove local finite-rank density and compute essential and finite-rank distances.
result: They establish endpoint ranges where boundedness implies compactness, characterize compactness via active-tail decay above boundaries, and identify the essential distance, finite-rank distance, and Hausdorff noncompactness radius with the coupled active tail.
conclusion: The paper provides a detailed functional-analytic classification of compactness and essential norms for weighted bilinear Hardy operators, including quasi-Banach targets and exact scalar transfers for finite left endpoints.

title: Advances In Continuous-Time Multiparametric Optimal Control: The Role Of Time-Varying Active Constraints
authors: Efstratios N. Pistikopoulos Lida Lamakani
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiparametric optimal control in continuous time partitions the space of initial states into critical regions, each with its own control law involving a set of time-varying active constraints. The boundaries between two neighbouring regions are either hyperplanes, which are given in closed form by one linear equation, or curved boundaries, which must be computed. The sequence of time-varying active constraints plays a key role in defining the linear or nonlinear shape of a critical-region boundary. In this paper we show how to determine that shape prior to any computation. In particular, we show that the boundary is a hyperplane under two conditions. First, the new constraint becomes active at the same instant at every point of the boundary. Second, the durations for which the other constraints stay active are the same at every point of the boundary. Otherwise, the boundary is curved. Both conditions can be read from the sequences of active constraints of the two neighbouring regions, which gives five rules, each yielding a hyperplane or a curved boundary. We illustrate the rules on the Newell-Lee evaporator, where they classify the eight boundaries of a seven-region partition into four hyperplanes, given in closed form, and four curved boundaries, computed exactly.
tldr: This paper studies continuous-time multiparametric optimal control, showing how the shape of critical-region boundaries can be determined from time-varying active-constraint sequences before computation.
motivation: Multiparametric optimal control partitions initial-state space into regions with distinct control laws, but the geometric form of region boundaries has been difficult to predict without solving the problem.
method: The authors derive five rules that classify each boundary as hyperplane or curved based on two conditions involving when new constraints activate and how long other constraints remain active, then apply them to the Newell-Lee evaporator.
result: For the Newell-Lee evaporator's seven-region partition, the rules correctly classify four boundaries as hyperplanes with closed-form equations and four as curved boundaries, which are computed exactly.
conclusion: The active-constraint sequence can predict boundary geometry prior to computation, simplifying multiparametric optimal control analysis.

title: Characterizing Identifiability In Boolean Factor Models
authors: Gongjun Xu Mengqi Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Boolean factor models, including prominent subfamilies such as Boolean matrix decompositions and cognitive diagnosis models, find broad applications ranging from social sciences to engineering. Despite their flexibility, a key challenge lies in establishing the identifiability of their graphical structures, which specify how latent variables influence observed variables. Existing identifiability conditions typically rely on the strong assumption of pure nodes, which may be unrealistic in many applications. We develop a novel approach leveraging the Hasse diagram to represent the distribution of observed variables and transform identifiability into a graph isomorphism challenge. Based on this, we establish {\it sufficient and necessary} graphical identifiability conditions that do not require pure nodes. We further derive equivalent algebraic conditions and develop an efficient Boolean satisfiability (SAT)-based verification algorithm. We extend the analysis to probabilistic Boolean factor models, establishing conditions for jointly identifying the graphical structure and additional model parameters without requiring pure nodes. Our results substantially broaden the class of identifiable and interpretable Boolean factor models by removing the pure-node requirement, yielding new theoretical insights, while also providing practitioners with a concrete and easily implementable tool to assess model identifiability.
tldr: The paper develops sufficient and necessary identifiability conditions for Boolean factor models without requiring pure nodes, using Hasse diagrams and graph isomorphism.
motivation: Boolean factor models are widely used but existing identifiability conditions depend on the strong and often unrealistic pure-node assumption.
method: It represents the distribution of observed variables via a Hasse diagram, transforms identifiability into a graph isomorphism problem, and derives algebraic conditions with a SAT-based verification algorithm.
result: The approach yields graphical and algebraic identifiability conditions that remove the pure-node requirement, and extends to probabilistic Boolean factor models.
conclusion: The work broadens the class of identifiable Boolean factor models and provides a practical tool for assessing model identifiability.

title: Asymptotic Approximation Of Sensitivities In Finite Dimensional Continuous Data Assimilation With Application To Parameter Estimation
authors: Jared P. Whitehead Joshua Newey
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a rigorous justification for a parameter estimation algorithm which couples continuous data assimilation to generic optimization. For finite dimensional systems, we provide a rigorous justification of an asymptotic approximation of the sensitivity for the underlying modeled dynamical system, prove that the [MATH] loss function satisfies an approximate Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality, and use that result to justify convergence of gradient descent for the proposed algorithm. Numerical examples are provided that demonstrate the precision of the rigorous results.
tldr: This paper develops rigorous convergence guarantees for a parameter estimation algorithm that couples continuous data assimilation with gradient-based optimization in finite-dimensional dynamical systems.
motivation: Parameter estimation in continuous data assimilation is important for improving model accuracy, but rigorous justification of optimization-based approaches has been limited.
method: The authors prove an asymptotic approximation of sensitivities for the underlying modeled dynamical system, establish that the loss function satisfies an approximate Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality, and use this to justify convergence of gradient descent.
result: Numerical examples demonstrate the precision of the theoretical results and support the convergence analysis.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous foundation for coupling continuous data assimilation with generic optimization for parameter estimation in finite-dimensional settings.

title: Property-Preserving Data Compression For Incompressible Flows
authors: Andrey Pluzhnik, Ramansh Sharma, Martin Burtscher, Varun Shankar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a method for lossy compression of incompressible (i.e., divergence-free) velocity fields that preserves zero divergence and, on periodic domains, periodicity. We fit the nodal velocities with property-preserving matrix-valued kernels and compress their coefficients using standard lossy compressors. Every decompressed coefficient vector defines a field with the same constraints, independently of the compression tolerance. We present several fitting schemes designed around either low-rank representation of or sparsity in the interpolation matrix. More specifically, we show results for global Mat\'ern interpolation, a two-level Nystr\"om approximation, Nystr\"om--Wendland residual interpolation, multilevel Wendland interpolation and a property-preserving (redundant) kernel frame. We derive nodal error bounds that relate the compressor tolerance to the additional velocity error. Experiments with four compressors on cavity, Taylor--Green, and species-transport flows verify the bounds under their coefficient-error assumptions and compare storage at matched velocity accuracy. The low-rank methods give compact representations when they resolve the velocity field sufficiently accurately; residual, multilevel, and frame interpolation extend the attainable accuracy when they do not. We also measure changes in turbulent velocity statistics. The resulting representations support an accuracy--compression tradeoff while preserving incompressibility and periodicity analytically.
tldr: The paper introduces lossy compression methods for incompressible velocity fields that analytically preserve zero divergence and periodicity by fitting matrix-valued kernels and compressing coefficients.
motivation: Incompressible flow simulations and data analysis require storing velocity fields compactly, but standard lossy compressors may break physical constraints like divergence-free and periodic boundary conditions.
method: The authors fit nodal velocities with property-preserving matrix-valued kernels (Matern, Nystrom, Wendland, multilevel, and frame schemes), then compress the coefficients with standard lossy compressors; decompression always yields fields satisfying the constraints.
result: Experiments on cavity, Taylor-Green, and species-transport flows with four compressors show that low-rank methods give compact representations when accurate, while residual, multilevel, and frame interpolation extend attainable accuracy; turbulent statistics are also measured.
conclusion: The approach provides an accuracy-compression tradeoff while exactly preserving incompressibility and periodicity, supported by nodal error bounds linking compressor tolerance to velocity error.

title: Finding Stationary Points Under Higher-Order Smoothness: Trapping Algorithms And First-Order Lower Bounds
authors: Huanjian Zhou, Masashi Sugiyama, Taiji Suzuki
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the query complexity of finding approximate stationary points under higher-order smoothness using only function values or only gradients. Our results cover different dimensions, oracle models, randomization, and constraints. For constant dimension [MATH] and [MATH] objectives, with [MATH], we give deterministic function-value gradient trapping algorithms with query complexities [MATH] on [MATH] and [MATH] on [MATH]. High-order line integration enables gradient-only trapping. For two-dimensional [MATH] objectives, randomized integration yields [MATH] gradient queries on [MATH], breaking the deterministic gradient-only [MATH] barrier. For general dimension, we introduce a trapping-or-descent framework that lazily reuses boundary models. For [MATH] objectives with [MATH], it achieves deterministic query complexities [MATH] using function values and [MATH] using gradients. These bounds apply to approximate stationary points on [MATH] and approximate KKT points on [MATH]. Their dimension-independent accuracy exponent matches the classical AR[MATH] exponent [MATH] when [MATH]. For sufficiently high dimension, we prove randomized lower bounds for gradient-only methods. For [MATH] objectives, our lower bound is [MATH], matching known upper bounds for [MATH] and, up to logarithmic factors, for [MATH]. Without the [MATH] assumption, we obtain an [MATH] lower bound for every fixed [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies query complexity for finding approximate stationary points under higher-order smoothness using function values or gradients, with new trapping algorithms and lower bounds.
motivation: The authors aim to improve understanding of how smoothness assumptions affect the difficulty of finding stationary points in optimization, covering deterministic and randomized settings.
method: They develop gradient trapping and trapping-or-descent frameworks that reuse boundary models, and prove randomized lower bounds for gradient-only methods.
result: They obtain deterministic and randomized query complexities for constant and general dimensions, including a two-dimensional randomized gradient method that breaks a deterministic barrier and matching lower bounds in the high-dimensional regime.
conclusion: The results characterize fundamental limits of stationary point finding under higher-order smoothness, with implications for optimization algorithm design but no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: When Can An Infinite-Stream Evaluation Support Dynamic Programming? Compatibility, Recursive Compression, And Generalized Summation
authors: Yingzhe Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic programming for nonstandard infinite-horizon criteria requires more than finite stream values: one-step control substitutions must remain evaluable, and continuation information must propagate recursively. For expected stage-reward streams, we separate domain admissibility, finite-dimensional continuous autonomous realizability, scalar sufficiency, and contextual order consistency. For absolutely summable weighted criteria, we prove that the minimum Euclidean dimension of an exact continuous autonomous continuation state equals the temporal Hankel rank. Thus finite Hankel rank exactly characterizes when temporal nonstationarity can be replaced by finite endogenous state augmentation; the lower bound applies even to nonlinear continuous encoders and already holds in a one-state MDP. For literal Candelpergher Ramanujan summation, the same common-continuation test fails earlier: changing only the current action can leave the evaluation domain. Abel summation provides a contrasting prefix-closed benchmark.
tldr: The paper characterizes when infinite-stream evaluations can support dynamic programming by separating compatibility, recursive compression, and generalized summation conditions, with temporal Hankel rank as the exact dimension of a continuous autonomous continuation state.
motivation: Dynamic programming for nonstandard infinite-horizon criteria requires more than finite stream values: one-step control substitutions must remain evaluable, and continuation information must propagate recursively.
method: It separates domain admissibility, finite-dimensional continuous autonomous realizability, scalar sufficiency, and contextual order consistency, then proves a dimension-Hankel-rank equality for absolutely summable weighted criteria and tests literal Candelpergher Ramanujan summation against Abel summation.
result: The minimum Euclidean dimension of an exact continuous autonomous continuation state equals the temporal Hankel rank, so finite Hankel rank exactly characterizes when temporal nonstationarity can be replaced by finite endogenous state augmentation; the bound holds even for nonlinear encoders and one-state MDPs, while Ramanujan summation fails the common-continuation test earlier.
conclusion: The work provides mathematical foundations for recursive infinite-stream evaluation in dynamic programming and generalized summation, but it does not contribute to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Azumaya Descent And \'etale-local Cyclotomic Comparison: A Noncommutative Filtration
authors: Alexander Zuevsky H\^ong V\^an L\^e
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bhatt-Morrow-Scholze motivic filtration on topological Hochschild homology ([MATH]) is extended to Azumaya algebras over quasisyntomic rings. We prove the Azumaya descent theorem: [MATH] of such an algebra is equivalent, as an underlying spectrum, to [MATH] of its center, normalized on [MATH] by the reduced trace instead of the unit map. This comparison [MATH] is not shown to be \'etale-locally cyclotomic. But what is cyclotomic \'etale-locally is a separate Morita trace, agreeing with [MATH] only on [MATH]. The resulting transported filtration is exactly the center BMS filtration, well defined up to the automorphism ambiguity of [MATH]. It is insensitive to the Brauer class, reflected instead by [MATH]-theoretic and module-categorical pairings [MATH] does not see. We establish the analogous statement for derived Azumaya algebras over connective [MATH]-rings, under a connectivity hypothesis.
tldr: The paper extends the Bhatt-Morrow-Scholze motivic filtration to Azumaya algebras over quasisyntomic rings and proves an Azumaya descent theorem relating topological Hochschild homology to that of the center.
motivation: The authors aim to generalize the BMS motivic filtration, a central tool in p-adic Hodge theory and algebraic K-theory, to noncommutative settings via Azumaya algebras.
method: They establish an Azumaya descent theorem using reduced trace normalization, and analyze étale-local cyclotomic comparison for a separate Morita trace, transporting the filtration to the center.
result: The topological Hochschild homology of an Azumaya algebra is equivalent to that of its center, with the resulting filtration matching the center's BMS filtration up to automorphism, and being insensitive to the Brauer class.
conclusion: The work provides a noncommutative filtration framework and extends the analogous statement to derived Azumaya algebras over connective rings under a connectivity hypothesis.

title: Mirror: Multipath Quorum Integrity For Llm Multi-Agent Communication
authors: Ryuichi Yamafuji Lun, Jingzhen Wang, Shreyas Kolte, Ruiteng Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inter-agent communication is central to Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-MAS), but it introduces an underexplored vulnerability: Agent-in-the-Middle (AiTM) attacks that manipulate messages in transit without compromising the agents themselves. Prior work reports Attack Success Rates (ASR) approaching 100% on structured tasks. Existing defenses rely on semantic validation, which requires additional inference and can block benign outputs, or on transport-layer encryption, which does not help when an intermediary legitimately terminates TLS. We present MIRROR, a communication-layer integrity primitive that replicates a single canonicalized payload across k logical routes and accepts a message only when a strict majority of routes report the same digest. MIRROR uses unkeyed hashing and so authenticates nothing on its own, since an active on-path adversary can always recompute a digest over a payload it has modified. All integrity derives from the assumption that honest routes form a majority. The digest serves only to make witness routes constant-size and to bind the recovered payload to the quorum-agreed value under second-preimage resistance. We give the guarantee under a route-compromise bound alpha < 0.5, and extend it to correlated routes, where the quantity that matters is the size of the largest shared-failure group and not the route count. We further show that availability and integrity degrade at the same threshold: below alpha = 0.5, quorum-denial and message-dropping adversaries cannot block honest traffic. Across MMLU, HumanEval, and MBPP on two frameworks and four communication topologies, and in a MetaGPT deployment against a production API, MIRROR reduces ASR to 0% below the threshold at 1x LLM token cost. LLM-as-a-Judge costs 35x in the same deployment, and blocks up to 44.2% of benign outputs in the topology sweep.
tldr: MIRROR is a communication-layer integrity primitive that replicates payloads across multiple routes and accepts messages only when a strict majority report the same digest, defending LLM multi-agent systems against agent-in-the-middle attacks.
motivation: Inter-agent communication in LLM multi-agent systems is vulnerable to agent-in-the-middle attacks that can manipulate messages without compromising agents, and existing semantic or transport-layer defenses are either costly or ineffective.
method: The protocol canonicalizes a payload and sends it over k logical routes, requiring a quorum of matching unkeyed digests for acceptance; integrity derives from an honest-route majority assumption alpha < 0.5, with extensions to correlated routes and shared-failure groups.
result: Across MMLU, HumanEval, and MBPP on multiple frameworks and topologies, MIRROR reduces attack success rates to 0% below the compromise threshold at 1x LLM token cost, while LLM-as-a-Judge costs 35x and blocks up to 44.2% of benign outputs.
conclusion: MIRROR provides a lightweight multipath quorum integrity mechanism for LLM-MAS with availability and integrity guarantees under honest-majority route assumptions, but it is a classical AI-security contribution unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Hop-Decayed Influence: New Vulnerabilities Of Structural Auxiliary Indexing In GraphRAG Pipelines With Llm
authors: Jisung Park, John Le, Heath Cooper
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GraphRAG pipelines construct auxiliary structures during offline indexing--semantic summaries, hierarchical edges, and pre-computed scores--that determine how retrieval is prioritised at query time. Prior attacks target only instance-level components (nodes, edges, triples), overlooking these schema-level structures. We formalise Auxiliary Schema-Level Entity as a novel attack surface and propose the 3S Framework (Semantics, Structure, Scoring) for its systematic exploitation. Our Hop-Decayed Influence (HDI) attack identifies high-impact targets through query-aware influence propagation and corrupts their auxiliary structures post-indexing. Across two benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA) and two architectures (Microsoft GraphRAG, HippoRAG2), HDI achieves 88-94% attack success rate while modifying as few as 0.016% of auxiliary structures. Each modification affects up to 6.00 queries (Schema Leverage Ratio), demonstrating 1:N amplification unavailable to instance-level attacks. Manipulated structures evade perplexity and paraphrase defenses with over 99% evasion rate, as they remain linguistically coherent system-generated artifacts. These results reveal that auxiliary schema-level entities receive implicit trust without runtime validation, constituting a structural blind spot in current GraphRAG defenses. [URL].
tldr: This paper identifies auxiliary schema-level entities in GraphRAG pipelines as a new attack surface and introduces the Hop-Decayed Influence (HDI) attack to corrupt them with high success and evasion rates.
motivation: Prior attacks on GraphRAG focus only on instance-level components such as nodes, edges, and triples, while ignoring the schema-level structures like semantic summaries and precomputed scores that guide retrieval prioritization.
method: The authors formalize Auxiliary Schema-Level Entity as an attack surface, propose the 3S Framework (Semantics, Structure, Scoring) for exploitation, and design HDI to identify high-impact targets via query-aware influence propagation and modify their post-indexing auxiliary structures.
result: Across HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA with Microsoft GraphRAG and HippoRAG2, HDI achieves 88-94% attack success while modifying only 0.016% of auxiliary structures, with each modification affecting up to 6.00 queries, and over 99% evasion of perplexity and paraphrase defenses.
conclusion: Auxiliary schema-level entities receive implicit trust without runtime validation, creating a structural blind spot in current GraphRAG defenses that enables amplified and stealthy attacks.

title: Mitigating Private Data Leakage In LLMs With Whiteout
authors: Anna Yoo Jeong Ha, Ronik Bhaskar, Haitao Zheng, Ben Y. Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) are trained on massive, largely unfiltered datasets, including content scraped from nearly every accessible website and user inputs. As a result, LLMs often memorize and reproduce personally sensitive information (PSI) such as birth dates, phone numbers, and home addresses. This leads to significant privacy risks, particularly for high-profile individuals such as executives, politicians, and judges. Existing mitigations largely rely on machine unlearning. However, these methods often remove more information than needed, degrade model utility and safety, and are highly vulnerable to attacks. This paper presents Whiteout, a practical tool that, upon requests by individuals, prevents LLMs from regurgitating their genuine PSIs, by overwriting them using precise and carefully designed obfuscation samples. We evaluate Whiteout on modern LLMs of varying sizes and makers, including a widely-used OpenAI model. Results show that Whiteout effectively prevents disclosure of the targeted PSIs, has negligible impact on model utility and safety, and outperforms existing alternatives. We also test Whiteout against a wide range of countermeasures, from black-box attacks like jailbreaking to white-box adaptive attacks like relearning and quantization. Finally, we conclude with a discussion on the security and ethical implications of Whiteout.
tldr: Whiteout is a tool that prevents LLMs from reproducing an individual's personally sensitive information by overwriting it with carefully designed obfuscation samples.
motivation: LLMs memorize and expose personally sensitive information from training data, creating privacy risks for high-profile individuals, while existing unlearning methods over-remove information, degrade utility, and are vulnerable to attacks.
method: Whiteout uses precise obfuscation samples to overwrite targeted private data upon individual requests, and is evaluated on modern LLMs of varying sizes and makers including an OpenAI model.
result: Whiteout effectively prevents disclosure of targeted PSIs with negligible impact on model utility and safety, outperforming existing alternatives, and resists a wide range of black-box and white-box countermeasures.
conclusion: Whiteout offers a practical privacy mitigation for LLMs, and the paper discusses its security and ethical implications.

title: SideKernel: A Usable microVM Sandbox For Ai Coding Agents On macOS
authors: Dimitrios Prasakis
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding agents are untrusted system components, yet they require autonomy on the developer machines they run on. This contradiction is a security problem. Sandboxes provide an isolated environment, but for local macOS development, the existing local, open-source options for AI coding agents are few in number and cumbersome to use. I conducted a formative online user survey which indicates that fewer than 40% of AI coding agent users run their agents in a sandbox and identifies the top usability barriers hindering AI coding agent sandbox adoption. These findings are used to develop SideKernel: an open-source, local, microVM-based macOS sandbox for AI coding agents designed for usability. To evaluate SideKernel, I compiled a list of sandboxes available on the market and filtered it against five inclusion criteria. Then I performed a comparative analysis between SideKernel and the sandboxes that satisfy these criteria, across 23 capability tests derived from the usability barriers revealed by the user survey. I discovered that only a few sandboxes are similar to SideKernel, and that among those, Docker Sandboxes and SideKernel score highest on capability features related to usability. A secondary contribution of this paper is a survey of the existing solution space for local, open-source, microVM-based macOS sandboxes for AI coding agents.
tldr: SideKernel is an open-source microVM-based macOS sandbox designed to improve the usability of isolating AI coding agents, evaluated against existing sandboxes via 23 capability tests derived from a user survey.
motivation: AI coding agents are untrusted components that need autonomy on developer machines, but existing local macOS sandbox options are few and cumbersome, and fewer than 40% of users adopt sandboxing.
method: A formative online user survey identifies usability barriers, then SideKernel is built as a microVM sandbox; it is compared against market-available sandboxes filtered by five inclusion criteria across 23 capability tests.
result: Few sandboxes are similar to SideKernel, and among those, Docker Sandboxes and SideKernel score highest on usability-related capability features.
conclusion: SideKernel provides a usable local macOS microVM sandbox for AI coding agents and includes a survey of the existing local open-source solution space.

title: Proving At Scale For Universal Algebra
authors: Jo\~{a}o Ara\'{u}jo, Jan H\r{u}la, Mikol\'{a}\v{s} Janota, Edmond W. H. Lee, Bartosz Naskr\k{e}cki
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce SemiBase, a project that computes and formally certifies finite identity bases for small semigroups. Deciding finite basability is undecidable for finite algebras and remains open for finite semigroups. The task requires a proof that a candidate basis is complete, or a proof that none exists, rather than a single first-order validity query. LLM-guided agents search for these proofs; a referee agent rebuilds them from source, and the Lean kernel checks the resulting corpus in a final audit. Humans choose targets and approve final outcomes. We certify every semigroup of order at most 6: all 1309 semigroups of order at most 5 and all 15973 of order 6, including proofs that the four known nonfinitely based semigroups have no finite basis. The bases for order 6 define 505 distinct varieties, whose inclusion order Vampire determines except for four pairs. The resulting catalogue is a machine-checked account of results scattered across the literature and a tested foundation for order 7.
tldr: SemiBase computes and formally certifies finite identity bases for small semigroups, covering all semigroups of order up to 6 using LLM-guided proof search and Lean verification.
motivation: Deciding finite basability is undecidable for finite algebras and open for finite semigroups; the task requires finding completeness or nonexistence proofs rather than single first-order validity queries.
method: LLM-guided agents search for proofs, a referee agent rebuilds them from source, and the Lean kernel checks the resulting corpus in a final audit, with humans choosing targets and approving outcomes.
result: All 1309 semigroups of order at most 5 and all 15973 of order 6 are certified, including proofs that the four known nonfinitely based semigroups have no finite basis; order 6 bases define 505 distinct varieties.
conclusion: The catalogue provides a machine-checked account of scattered literature results and a tested foundation for order 7.

title: Out Of Sync, Out Of Sight: Phantom State Attacks Against IIoT Intrusion Detection
authors: Sabrine Ennaji, Elhadj Benkhelifa, Nadia Kabachi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning-based intrusion detection systems (IDS) are critical for securing Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environments. Most adversarial research against them perturbs the feature vector or the traffic that produces it, and depends on gradient access, repeated model queries, or a learned model of benign traffic. A smaller line of work reshapes packet timing without querying the detector, but makes malicious traffic mimic a learned model of benign timing. Across these approaches, one assumption of industrial monitoring pipelines has received little attention: temporal synchronization. An IDS reconstructs operational state by aggregating telemetry into sliding or tumbling windows, so its view depends not only on what is observed but on when each observation falls relative to a window boundary. We introduce the Phantom State Attack (PSA), which exploits that dependence under a passive, zero-query threat model. Rather than modifying packets, perturbing features, querying the classifier, or fitting any model of benign traffic, PSA injects bounded timing drift calibrated to the attack flow's own inter-arrival variability, moving observations across the nearest window boundary by the minimal shift needed. The IDS then reconstructs a phantom state that diverges from the true process state. We evaluate PSA on ToN-IoT and CIC IIoT 2025 (DataSense), against Random Forest, MLP and XGBoost, measuring detection degradation, synchronization distortion, stealth, and attacker cost. PSA degrades detection on flows carrying enough packets for window-boundary redistribution, and leaves others almost unchanged, so its effect is conditional. A query-based baseline reaches higher raw success but needs many queries per window, while PSA needs none. The results identify temporal aggregation as an attack surface reachable under weaker assumptions than prior evasion techniques.
tldr: The paper introduces Phantom State Attack, a passive zero-query timing-drift attack that exploits temporal window synchronization in IIoT intrusion detection systems to degrade detection by shifting observations across window boundaries.
motivation: Machine learning-based intrusion detection systems in IIoT rely on temporal aggregation into sliding or tumbling windows, but adversarial research has largely overlooked the security implications of this synchronization assumption.
method: PSA injects bounded timing drift calibrated to the attack flow's own inter-arrival variability, moving packets across the nearest window boundary without modifying packets, perturbing features, querying the classifier, or fitting a benign-traffic model.
result: Evaluated on ToN-IoT and CIC IIoT 2025 against Random Forest, MLP, and XGBoost, PSA degrades detection only for flows with enough packets for window-boundary redistribution, while a query-based baseline achieves higher raw success at the cost of many queries per window.
conclusion: Temporal aggregation is identified as an attack surface reachable under weaker assumptions than prior evasion techniques, highlighting a conditional but practical vulnerability in IIoT monitoring pipelines.

title: AgentTrap: Stateful Feedback Deception Against Autonomous Penetration Testing Agents
authors: Yuelin Wang, Jiongchi Yu, Yanbang Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous penetration testing agents conduct multi-step attacks by continuously adapting their plans and actions to target responses. As a common defense, honeypots can be deployed to divert these agents from real assets by presenting decoy services, while also supporting attack tracing and active counterattacks. However, conventional honeypots rely primarily on static artifacts and predefined responses, leaving them unable to adapt to the evolving attack strategies of autonomous penetration testing agents. To this end, we present AgentTrap, the first closed-loop honeypot tailored for autonomous penetration testing agents. AgentTrap uses sentinel endpoints to avoid benign interference, stateful deception grounded in the protected application, and behavior-guided escalation to sustain engagement and collect agent-side behavioral evidence with controlled disclosures. We evaluate AgentTrap against eight autonomous penetration-testing agents in a deployed web application containing a real application endpoint and a separate honeypot endpoint configured under three defense strategies. Compared with no defense, AgentTrap reduces the aggregate real-target attack success rate from 95.8% to 79.2% and successfully elicits attacker API keys in 18.8% of the runs, outperforming static deception and fixed escalation. Furthermore, trace analysis shows that resistance to such counterattacks depends jointly on model-level recognition of deceptive requests and architecture-level isolation of sensitive resources.
tldr: AgentTrap is a closed-loop honeypot system that uses stateful feedback deception to engage and counter autonomous penetration-testing agents.
motivation: Conventional honeypots rely on static artifacts and predefined responses, making them ill-suited to adapt to the continuously evolving strategies of autonomous penetration-testing agents.
method: The system employs sentinel endpoints to avoid benign interference, stateful deception grounded in the protected application, and behavior-guided escalation to sustain attacker engagement while collecting behavioral evidence via controlled disclosures.
result: Against eight autonomous penetration-testing agents, AgentTrap reduced the aggregate real-target attack success rate from 95.8% to 79.2% and elicited attacker API keys in 18.8% of runs, outperforming static deception and fixed escalation.
conclusion: Resistance to such counterattacks depends jointly on model-level recognition of deceptive requests and architecture-level isolation of sensitive resources, highlighting key considerations for securing autonomous agent deployments.

title: Digital Twin-Assisted Mapping Of Ics Telemetry To Att&ck For Ics With Evidence-Driven Dependency Reasoning
authors: Konstantinos E. Kampourakis, Vyron Kampourakis, Vasileios Gkioulos, Sokratis Katsikas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconstructing adversarial behavior from Industrial Control System (ICS) telemetry is difficult because process observations reveal physical changes more directly than the actions that produced them. This paper presents a Digital Twin (DT)-assisted framework that extracts synchronized state changes, converts them into evidence-preserving descriptions, maps them to ATT&CK for ICS through retrieval-augmented Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning, and constructs a typed dependency graph. Evaluation comprises a four-configuration ablation on nine held-out SWaT scenarios containing ten telemetry-evaluable ground-truth episodes, three independent generations of the principal mapping configurations, and external evaluation on BATADAL and WADI. Across the three SWaT generations, DT-enriched mapping produces fewer annotation-relative False Positive (FP) episodes in every run, with a mean per-run reduction of 34.1%. Both configurations obtain a mean recall of 0.633, although recall varies between 0.50 and 0.70 and DT enrichment does not improve F1 in every run. These observations are descriptive: the primary-run paired comparisons do not reach statistical significance, and the mapping advantage does not transfer to either external dataset. An exploratory positive-only dependency benchmark recovers eight of nine documented Co-occurrence relationships with DT context. A separate end-to-end benchmark containing one positive pair and 25 negative controls exposes propagation of mapping errors into unsupported edges. The findings identify both the potential and limitations of DT context for semantic security interpretation, without establishing reliable autonomous attribution, general causal reconstruction, or practical analyst benefit.
tldr: A Digital Twin-assisted framework maps ICS telemetry to ATT&CK for ICS using retrieval-augmented LLM reasoning and typed dependency graphs.
motivation: Reconstructing adversarial behavior from Industrial Control System telemetry is difficult because process observations reveal physical changes more directly than the actions that produced them.
method: The framework extracts synchronized state changes, converts them into evidence-preserving descriptions, maps them to ATT&CK for ICS through retrieval-augmented LLM reasoning, and constructs a typed dependency graph; it is evaluated on SWaT, BATADAL, and WADI.
result: DT-enriched mapping reduces annotation-relative false-positive episodes by a mean per-run 34.1% on SWaT, but paired comparisons lack statistical significance, recall averages 0.633, and the advantage does not transfer to external datasets.
conclusion: The findings identify both the potential and limitations of DT context for semantic security interpretation, without establishing reliable autonomous attribution, general causal reconstruction, or practical analyst benefit.

title: Beyond Predefined Sinks: Security-Aware Dependency Analysis For Llm Agents
authors: Hang Cui
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly connect model-generated decisions to security-sensitive software capabilities such as command execution, filesystem access, network communication, browser control, and external tools. Existing analyses often use predefined sensitive operations as anchors, but operation identity alone is insufficient to determine security implications. We present AgentSecGraph, a security-aware static analysis framework that constructs a candidate-centered Security-Aware Agent Dependency Graph (Security-ADG) for each security-sensitive operation. It augments operation identity with agent relevance, source and dependency evidence, trust-boundary context, guard evidence, and external-effect semantics. We further introduce AgentSecBench, a corpus of 67 real-world LLM-agent repositories spanning 11 ecosystems and 37,542 source files. The current analyzer identifies 23,866 static security-sensitive operation candidates across 65 repositories and emits one Security-ADG artifact per candidate. Corpus-wide analysis recovers source-to-operation dependency evidence for 9,821 candidates (41.15%) and potential guard evidence for 3,075 (12.88%), completing in 50.8 minutes. Using a separate reproduction-backed evaluation layer, we establish 22 security-sensitive behaviors across 13 repositories: one confirmed vulnerability, one pending disclosure candidate, and 20 guarded behaviors. In nine held-out cases, Security-ADG preserves 91.1% of the reference context and all five observed guards, compared with 20.0% for a sink-only view and 40.0% for a simplified ADG. These results show that security-aware dependency and contextual evidence enable distinctions that cannot be recovered from sensitive-operation identity alone.
tldr: The paper presents AgentSecGraph, a security-aware static analysis framework that builds candidate-centered dependency graphs for security-sensitive operations in LLM agents, along with a benchmark of real-world repositories.
motivation: Existing analyses of LLM-agent security rely on predefined sensitive operations as anchors, but operation identity alone is insufficient to determine security implications.
method: The framework constructs a Security-Aware Agent Dependency Graph (Security-ADG) for each sensitive operation, incorporating agent relevance, source and dependency evidence, trust-boundary context, guard evidence, and external-effect semantics; it also introduces AgentSecBench, a corpus of 67 LLM-agent repositories.
result: The analyzer identifies 23,866 static security-sensitive operation candidates across 65 repositories, recovering source-to-operation dependency evidence for 41.15% and guard evidence for 12.88% of candidates, and in held-out cases Security-ADG preserves 91.1% of reference context versus 20.0% for a sink-only view.
conclusion: Security-aware dependency and contextual evidence enable distinctions that cannot be recovered from sensitive-operation identity alone, improving security analysis for LLM agents.

title: Securing Computer-Use Agents Against Branch Steering Attacks
authors: Giulio Zingrillo, Hanna Foerster, Ilia Shumailov, Yiren Zhao, Robert Mullins
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern Computer Use Agents (CUAs) directly interact with graphical user interfaces and execute third-party web tools, exposing them to indirect prompt injection across every rendered page and tool response. While the Dual-LLM pattern is the primary system-level architecture offering formal security guarantees - using an isolated Planner LLM (P-LLM) to fix execution paths before processing untrusted inputs via a Quarantined LLM (Q-LLM) - these guarantees break down in graphical environments. Because CUA interaction is inherently dynamic, plans cannot remain data-independent; they must branch based on anticipated runtime web content - covering all possible cases the agent may encounter. This exposes agents to branch steering attacks, where an adversary crafts untrusted data to coerce a CUA down a hazardous, pre-approved branch without injecting explicit instructions. We systematically study branch steering attacks and introduce STEER-Bench (101 tasks across 9 domains), showing high attack success against both standard (94.4%) and vanilla Dual-LLM (89.5%) CUAs. We then propose COBRA, an architecture that pairs trusted branching plans with ahead-of-time capability constraints, strictly bounding the parameters and destinations each branch may execute. On STEER-Bench, COBRA reduces attack success to 0% while retaining 97% benign utility.
tldr: The paper studies branch steering attacks on Computer Use Agents and proposes COBRA, an architecture with trusted branching plans and capability constraints that eliminates such attacks while preserving benign utility.
motivation: Dual-LLM architectures providing formal security guarantees break down in dynamic graphical environments, since execution plans must branch on anticipated runtime web content, opening a hole for adversaries to steer agents into hazardous pre-approved branches.
method: The authors formalize branch steering attacks, build STEER-Bench (101 tasks across 9 domains) to measure them, and design COBRA, which pairs trusted branching plans with ahead-of-time capability constraints bounding each branch's parameters and destinations.
result: Baseline CUAs suffer 94.4% attack success and vanilla Dual-LLM 89.5%, whereas COBRA reduces attack success to 0% while retaining 97% of benign utility on STEER-Bench.
conclusion: Constraining branching plans with pre-approved capability bounds yields strong security guarantees for agents operating in dynamic GUI environments without significant loss of functionality.

title: Performance Analysis Of Mr-noma With Arbitrary Number Of Users And Symbol Rates
authors: Zainab Khader, Arafat Al-Dweik, Emad Alsusa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper analytically investigates the bit error rate (BER) performance of downlink multi-rate (MR)-non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) over Nakagami-m fading channels for an arbitrary number of users and symbol rates. The analysis is first developed for a three-user case, then generalized to systems with more than three users, yielding an exact BER expression for the first detected user and an accurate closed-form approximations for the remaining users under the perfect-successive interference cancellation (SIC) assumption. These results are further unified into a general average-BER expression over Nakagami-m fading for arbitrary user numbers and symbol-rate configurations. A symbol-pattern-dependent signal-to-interference plus noise ratio (SINR) analysis further shows how the symbol-duration diversity enables inherent interference cancellation, explaining the BER advantage of MR-NOMA over conventional single-symbol rate (SR)-NOMA. An average BER minimization problem is also formulated and numerically solved to optimize the users' power allocation, with simulation results corroborating the analytical findings. Overall, MR-NOMA is shown to offer greater flexibility in user pairing while maintaining reliable BER performance and accommodating diverse quality-of-service (QoS) requirements.
tldr: The paper analyzes the bit error rate performance of multi-rate non-orthogonal multiple access (MR-NOMA) over Nakagami-m fading channels for arbitrary numbers of users and symbol rates.
motivation: The authors aim to generalize BER analysis for MR-NOMA beyond three users and to understand how symbol-duration diversity enables inherent interference cancellation, improving over conventional single-symbol-rate NOMA.
method: They derive exact BER for the first detected user and closed-form approximations for others under perfect SIC, then unify into a general average-BER expression; they also formulate and numerically solve a power allocation optimization problem.
result: MR-NOMA is shown to offer greater flexibility in user pairing while maintaining reliable BER, and symbol-pattern-dependent SINR analysis explains its advantage over single-symbol-rate NOMA.
conclusion: The paper provides analytical tools and optimization for MR-NOMA in classical wireless communications, but it has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Data-Driven Static Output-Feedback Control For Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Paul Serna-Torre, Adam Sedlak, Patricia Hidalgo-Gonzalez
abstract: ArXiv:2610.02623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work proposes a data-driven framework that synthesizes output-feedback control for linear time-invariant multi-agent systems (MAS). We first develop two algorithms that use offline data samples of state and input trajectories to determine a Nash equilibrium (NE) for MAS. Next, we formulate a semidefinite program that, given the NE solution, computes the static output-feedback controllers for the agents in MAS. Compared to prior work, virtues of our framework include weaker controllability assumptions, the absence of online information and data-driven estimation of states. Next, we use the proposed framework to design control schemes for voltage and frequency regulation for nonlinear multi-nodal electrical networks with grid-forming and grid-following inverters. Thus, compared to prior work that implements their data-driven frameworks in small-scale numerical examples, we validate the performance of our data-driven framework in high-fidelity nonlinear models of MAS.
